#4956. The future of onchain FX could start with users, not institutional liquidity

Onchain FX does not need to recreate the trillion-dollar institutional market to become useful. Real demand can make smaller markets work first.

Opinion by Michael Egorov, founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis

For a long time, the obvious way to think about onchain foreign exchange (FX) was to start at the top. Banks tokenize currencies, large financial institutions move their FX activity onchain and institutional liquidity naturally follows.

The end result? Blockchain-based FX eventually grows large enough to resemble its traditional counterpart. But that’s not necessarily how it is going to happen.

In fact, there are growing signs that onchain FX will develop in the exact opposite way — from the bottom up.

Stablecoins like Brazilian Digital (BRZ) or Monerium’s EURe can be quickly redeemed onchain and easily moved from digital wallets to bank accounts. They generate healthy trading activity as decentralized finance (DeFi) users swap them in decentralized exchange (DEX) pools.

Markets like this end up developing in real time around a practical user need, which is moving directly between digital currencies and fiat.

This is still just an early-stage example, but the use case and demand are real enough. Keyrock data shows that the majority of onchain stablecoin trades tied to emerging market currencies fall in the $1,000 to $10,000 range — modest amounts compared to institutional scale — but that’s precisely the point.

It shows how the market is building in the general direction of onchain FX to meet practical payment needs, not just large traders.

People and businesses need to move their money between currencies, and clearly, they are not content to wait for major traditional finance (TradFi) institutions to move their FX operations onto blockchain rails.

Related: Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts

There’s a pretty common assumption about onchain FX in that a market needs huge liquidity before it can become really useful. In practice, though, that’s not entirely true.

If there is genuine demand from someone who needs to exchange dollars into euros, Swiss francs or another currency, even a smaller pool can process those transactions and serve a real economic purpose.

Stablecoin DEX Trade Volume. Source: Keyrock Research

Onchain FX doesn’t need to become big before it becomes useful; instead, it can grow precisely because people are actually using it.

As a matter of fact, this is more or less what happened with stablecoins. They began as a relatively niche crypto-native use case, and yet today we already know them to be part of a much broader financial infrastructure.

Chainalysis recently shared data that shows cross-border stablecoin activity jumped to over $220 billion by mid-2026. That’s an almost 80% growth over the course of one year, proving that demand and activity are constantly on the rise. There is no reason onchain FX can’t follow a similar path.

This is actually the most practical side of this issue. Onchain FX obviously won’t be able to compete with the entire global foreign exchange market anytime soon; that’s still years away. But the more interesting question is what problems it can solve for someone who already has money onchain.

Today, you can exchange a USD stablecoin into a EUR stablecoin (or some other alternative) onchain and use that money for payments with relatively little trouble. In fact, doing it this way is often faster and cheaper than going with a classic international bank transfer.

Related: Circle’s ARC token sale lifts earnings as lower yields weigh on USDC income

The same logic applies to onchain FX. A fintech or crypto-card company does not need to recreate the entire institutional market; what they need is to move their customers’ funds efficiently between currencies.

When someone is trying to pay in a different currency, converting it can add costs to the operation, since it usually involves Visa or Mastercard, which charge around 1% in processing fees.

Onchain exchanges are a much better option here. If user funds are already living on blockchain rails, swapping USD stablecoins into EUR stablecoins can be done directly, without going through any extra intermediaries, which is both faster and less costly.

Banks will most likely remain important entry and exit points where digital money needs to interact with the real world. Issuing and redeeming local currencies, accessing bank accounts, dealing with compliance and such is where banks will take the lead.

But when the money is actually onchain, many of the traditional “in-between” steps can be dropped for greater efficiency.

From the perspective of a user who just wants to conduct a financial transfer with minimal complications, that’s a highly positive improvement. How big or small the overall market matters little in this case.

Real demand is crucial, but it does not magically solve the problem of liquidity. The challenge is not simply to create a EUR/USD or CHF/USD pool; it’s to make them economically sustainable.

This is where automated market makers can make a difference. Traditional market-making firms may not find it attractive to provide liquidity for a small FX market; there may simply not be enough volume to justify the operational costs.

Cross-border stablecoin flows. Source: Chainalysys

Automated liquidity changes that equation because software can provide liquidity continuously without requiring a market-making firm to manually manage every trade.

Imagine two dollar stablecoins, USDC (USDC) and Tether (USDT). From the perspective of a traditional exchange, moving from one dollar stablecoin into another might look like a fairly boring business. Both assets are supposed to be worth roughly $1, so there isn’t much price movement to trade around.

But if there is still a real need for people to switch between stablecoins like that, an automated market maker can create a pool where users can make that swap directly. Each trade generates a small fee for the liquidity providers, and when enough people need the same conversion, a market can exist even when it doesn’t look particularly exciting to a traditional market maker.

This kind of adoption cannot exactly be called explosive, true, but there’s also nothing wrong with slow, natural growth. Sometimes, new markets just need a small group of people who have a problem the existing infrastructure does not solve particularly well. If those users can make the market economically viable, liquidity can grow from there.

About the author: Michael Egorov is the founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis. He is also a physicist, entrepreneur and crypto maximalist. Michael transitioned from the scientific field to the crypto industry and holds a bronze medal from the International Physics Olympiad and a PhD in ultracold atoms.

#4954. South Korea to publish draft of comprehensive crypto legal framework this week

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The draft is expected to include a licensing regime for crypto businesses and a bank-centered issuance system for local stablecoins.

South Korea's Financial Services Commission is preparing to release the government's draft for the Digital Asset Basic Act later this week, according to multiple local news reports.

The act is expected to become the country's second major piece of crypto legislation following the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which took effect in 2024. While that earlier legislation focused primarily on protecting user assets and preventing unfair market activities, the upcoming bill aims to provide clearer rules for the industry.

Authorities have previously indicated that the Digital Asset Basic Act would cover the legal definition of digital assets and comprehensive rules governing issuance and distribution. The draft is also expected to introduce a licensing regime for crypto businesses, shifting from the current notification system.

A more contested element of the bill is a proposed cap on ownership stakes held by major shareholders of crypto exchanges, widely reported to be in the range of 15% to 20%, to curb concentration risk. The measure has drawn strong opposition from the industry, with critics arguing that it would undermine free-market principles and property rights.

After the FSC releases the draft, it is expected to be merged with proposals from lawmakers and proceed to the National Assembly for further review and discussion.

​​Meanwhile, stablecoins are another major focus of the legislation. This follows South Korean President Lee Jae-myung calling for a local currency-based stablecoin market to protect the nation's monetary sovereignty in the digital age.

The government draft is expected to stipulate a bank-centered consortium model for issuing Korean won-pegged stablecoins, where banks would hold more than 50% in the consortium.

The country's central bank has pushed for this bank-first structure, having previously expressed concerns that unchecked stablecoin issuance could undermine monetary stability. This has also drawn backlash from local industry players who argued that setting this rule would deter innovation.

Other provisions in the bill are expected to further clarify different types of businesses, governance and internal controls of crypto projects, and establish conduct standards comparable to those for traditional financial companies. It would also further strengthen user protection requirements, including rules on asset segregation and operational safety.

#4952. Cross River Bank Launches Its First Bitcoin-Backed Loans With LendingUSA

Cross River Bank has launched its first bitcoin-backed loans, working with consumer lender LendingUSA to let eligible borrowers take out between $10,000 and $250,000 against their BTC without selling it.

The program is the first time Cross River has originated bitcoin-secured loans itself, according to The Block. LendingUSA runs the application platform, and every loan is made by Cross River, a New Jersey state-chartered bank, according to LendingUSA.

Borrowers can choose a loan-to-value ratio of 30%, 50% or 70%, which sets how much cash they receive against the value of the bitcoin they pledge. LendingUSA defines the ratio as the loan balance divided by the value of the collateral, so a 50% loan against $100,000 of bitcoin would be $50,000. Two repayment options are offered: interest-only or no monthly payments.

On an interest-only loan, borrowers make smaller monthly payments that roughly cover interest, with the principal and any remaining interest due at the end of the term. On a no-monthly-payment loan, the full balance plus interest is due at the end. LendingUSA says borrowers can repay early without penalties or fees.

Applicants go through a soft credit check, and LendingUSA says approval rests on the crypto being pledged rather than a credit score. The company says funding typically arrives within one to three business days after the collateral is verified.

A qualified third-party custodian holds the bitcoin for the life of the loan. Once the loan is repaid in full, the collateral is released back to the borrower, according to the company.

The terms carry the usual risk of borrowing against a volatile asset. LendingUSA says that if the value of the bitcoin falls, the loan-to-value ratio rises, and borrowers may be asked to add collateral or pay down the debt to avoid liquidation. The company says it will try to notify borrowers first but cannot guarantee it during fast price moves.

The timing matters. Bitcoin was trading near $61,000 on Monday morning, so a borrower at the 70% tier would have far less room before a collateral call than one at the 30% tier. Lower ratios leave a bigger cushion but unlock less cash per bitcoin pledged.

LendingUSA markets the loans for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and large purchases. The company says it has served more than 200,000 borrowers across its lending business, and the crypto product is its first expansion into digital asset-backed loans.

Cross River President Evan Russo framed the launch as a natural extension of the bank’s work. “Digital assets have become a meaningful part of how many consumers build and hold wealth, and the financial system must evolve to serve them responsibly,” Russo said in a statement.

“Cross River was built on the belief that innovation and trusted infrastructure go hand in hand,” he added. “Launching our first Bitcoin-secured lending program as the loan originator is a natural extension of that mission.”

The move adds a state-chartered bank to a lending market that has been moving closer to traditional finance. In August, Coinbase and Better Mortgage announced general availability of bitcoin-backed mortgages, and in April, Strike’s Jack Mallers announced lending proof-of-reserves and loans designed to withstand volatility.

Neither company has said how much bitcoin has been pledged so far or which custodian holds the collateral. LendingUSA’s page says rates and terms vary by applicant, and that loan amounts, interest rates and terms are disclosed once an application is received.

For now, the page lists the product’s maximum loan-to-value at 70%, and every loan on it is made by Cross River Bank.

The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, effective immediately, after what it called a series of discussions and meetings. Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, down 47.5% from its October high, which works out to roughly $2.7 trillion of market value gone in seven weeks. The company beat earnings last week and guided revenue higher, and the stock still fell 23% across the five sessions.

The Nasdaq dropped 10% on the week, its worst since 2020, erasing its entire 2026 gain and shedding about $8.7 trillion since October 6. The S&P and Dow both closed in correction, AMD lost 20.5%, and CoreWeave now trades below its IPO price. Bank of America’s fund manager survey showed investors cutting tech exposure by the most since 2006, with 52% expecting at least one major hyperscaler to announce a capex cut inside six months.

Polymarket traders put 54% odds that the AI bubble will burst in 2026.

Crypto rode the same elevator down. Bitcoin hit roughly $55,100 Friday night, its lowest level since 2024 and marking a new cycle low, 56% off last October’s peak. Fear and Greed printed 9 and ETFs bled $1.79 billion on the week. It’s now tracking toward two consecutive down years, which has never happened before.

Then came the weekend bounce. Bitcoin reclaimed $60,000 and sits over $61,000 this morning; ETH is back above $1,710, and even Anthropic, down 9% Friday, quotes near $90 on Hyperliquid’s perp, still above its $83 offer.

Two explanations landed over the weekend.

U.S. President Donald Trump posted Sunday that the market is down $6 trillion since the Democrats’ “rather strange” win on November 3, that the Nasdaq is down 20%, and that it’s “100% due to” Democratic policy. Looks like no Trump bailout is coming anytime soon.

Elon Musk’s version is more useful. He warned Saturday that the cash shortage next year is “going to be nuts,” because even a few months of lag between paying for compute and earning revenue off it means hundreds of billions in incremental working capital. Then the question: where will that come from?

That’s a funding problem rather than a valuation one, and it lands harder coming from him. SpaceX reportedly sold $32 billion of bonds last week to buy Nvidia chips, so he’s describing a squeeze he’s already borrowing into.

So where does this leave us? The Fed meets December 8th and 9th with the market pricing a hike into all of this. Gas prices just hit an eight-month low ahead of Thanksgiving, down about 15% in a month, which should take some pressure off the headline print. The catch is that pump prices are still running 18% above last year, and core CPI, the number Waller actually cited when he floated fifty basis points, strips energy out entirely. Any relief has to come from shelter and services cooling instead.

Perhaps the Fed provides some. Whether it’s enough to stop the bleeding, only time will tell.

#4938. Solo Bitcoin Miner Wins $191,000 Block Reward With Just 11 TH/s

A solo miner running about 11 terahashes per second has mined Bitcoin block 977,057, collecting a reward of 3.1287 BTC, or about $191,000, on a machine that makes up roughly one-millionth of a percent of the network.

The block was found through the solo service at CKpool on Sunday, Nov. 22, at about 7:54 a.m. ET. The reward is the 3.125 BTC subsidy plus about 0.0037 BTC in transaction fees, and it was worth roughly $191,000 at bitcoin’s price when the block landed.

The block holds 584 transactions. Its coinbase transaction pays 3.0661 BTC to a single address and 0.0626 BTC, about 2% of the reward, to a second output. That split matches the service’s 2% fee, which means the miner’s take is a little over $186,000.

Con Kolivas, the developer behind CKpool, congratulated the miner on X, whose address he abbreviated as bc1q~zy9j. It matches the end of the address that received the payout. Kolivas called it the 323rd block found on the service and “yet another lucky one.”

He said the miner had only about 11.1 TH/s of hashrate on a 3.47 TH worker. “A miner of this size has about a one in 1650 chance of solving a block in a year,” Kolivas wrote.

The block was tagged to Solo CK on the mempool.space block explorer, and its coinbase carries the pool’s signature. CKpool describes itself as a service that lets miners go after full solo blocks without running their own node, since you cannot mine directly to a Bitcoin Core node.

Solo CK has found five blocks since Nov. 6, according to the explorer’s pool page. The most recent before this one was block 976,642 on Nov. 19, followed by blocks on Nov. 11, Nov. 7 and Nov. 6. Each paid between 3.13 and 3.15 BTC.

Earlier this year, a different solo miner won block 943,411 on the same service on April 2, for about 3.139 BTC. In October, a FutureBit Apollo solo miner found block 973,262 and earned 3.154 BTC.

Those wins are the exception. Most of the network’s hashrate sits in large pools and industrial operations that split rewards across many miners, which is how they smooth out the luck. A single small machine can run for years without finding anything, and a lucky block can show up on day one. Miners on the service get nothing unless they find a block, and then they keep the full reward minus the 2% fee.

Bitcoin’s network hashrate was about 1.04 zettahashes per second, or roughly 1,043 exahashes, on a three-day average Monday. At 11.1 TH/s, the winning miner contributes about 0.000001% of that total, which fits Kolivas’s odds. One in 1,650 works out to a chance of about 0.06% over a full year of mining.

Mining difficulty is about 134.8 trillion. The last adjustment cut it by about 9.1%, and the next one, expected around Nov. 26, is estimated to raise it by about 9.2%, according to mempool.space. Difficulty resets every 2,016 blocks to keep blocks arriving about every 10 minutes.

Mining conditions have been tough. Bitcoin plunged to about $55,100 over the weekend before rebounding to near $64,000 on Monday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. Lower prices cut the dollar value of every block, whether it goes to an industrial miner or a hobbyist running a small solo rig.

The subsidy is fixed at 3.125 BTC until the next halving, so what the solo winner earns depends on fees and the market. A 3.1287 BTC block was worth about $196,000 at Monday’s price near $62,700, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $62,700.

#4937. Solo bitcoin miner beats the odds to win $191,000 block reward

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The miner reported just 11.1 TH/s on Solo CKPool, with an estimated one-in-1,650 chance of finding a block in a year.

A solo bitcoin miner beat the odds to solve a block carrying nearly $191,000 in rewards on Sunday.

The miner collected a total of 3.129 BTC ($190,764) for mining block 977,057, using solo bitcoin-mining software from CKpool, according to data from Bitcoin explorer Mempool. That comprised the 3.125 BTC block subsidy reward ($190,538) and 0.004 BTC ($226) in transaction fees, before CKpool's 2% fee.

"Congratulations to miner bc1q~zy9j for solving the 323rd block - yet another lucky one at EU solo.ckpool.org with only ~11.1 TH of hashrate on a 3.47 TH worker," CKpool developer Con Kolivas posted on X. "A miner of this size has about a one in 1650 chance of solving a block in a year."

The reported 11.1 TH/s is comparable to the combined output of a few home desktop miners, significantly smaller than top mining machines like Bitmain's U3S23H Antminer, with 1,160 TH/s. In comparison, top public bitcoin miners Bitdeer (BTDR), MARA Holdings (MARA), and Riot (RIOT) manage a hashrate of approximately 82.3 EH/s, 71.2 EH/s, and 37.2 EH/s, respectively, according to Ziven data. Those figures are approximately 7.4 million times, 6.4 million times, and 3.4 million times greater than the solo miner's hashrate.

The solo miner's hashpower is equivalent to about 0.000001% of the Bitcoin network's total estimated hashrate of 1.07 ZH/s on Nov. 23, per Mempool's data, which measures the total computational power dedicated to the network.

Smaller Bitcoin miners usually join shared pools to earn steady, proportional rewards since solo mining has an extremely low chance of winning a block. However, some try solo pools instead for a shot at the full block reward, hoping for a big, lottery-esque win despite the odds.

While CKpool is technically a mining pool, it is not used in the conventional sense where miners combine their hashrate for a better chance at block discovery by collaborating and sharing the rewards. Instead, miners using the solo CKpool work independently, keeping the full block reward if they find one, minus CKpool’s 2% fee. It avoids the need to run your own full node and pool infrastructure, making it a simple setup compared to true solo mining.

However, it's not the first time a solo miner has won Bitcoin blocks.

In April, another miner using CKpool in a solo mining configuration collected roughly $210,000 for mining block 943,411. A miner of that size has roughly a 1-in-28,000 chance of finding a block on any given day, Kolivas said at the time.

In November 2025, another solo miner reporting just 6 TH/s won a block worth around $265,000 at the time.

Solo miners with more substantial managed or rented hashrates have also found several Bitcoin blocks in recent years.

Public Citizen traced 66 of 130 qualifying wallets to exchanges that restrict US users, raising questions over who is attending Trump’s memecoin dinner on Sunday.

More than half the wallets that qualified for Donald Trump’s memecoin dinner on Sunday received TRUMP tokens from crypto exchanges that bar US users, according to analysis from consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Trump is hosting his second dinner for his top memecoin holders at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, more than a year after an inaugural dinner in May 2025. The dinner offers up to 185 seats based on time-weighted TRUMP holdings.

Public Citizen said it traced 66 of the 130 wallets on the public leaderboard to exchanges including Binance (the global exchange), Bybit and BloFin — which are not permitted to serve US citizens. The list also included 15 of the 29 wallets that qualified for a VIP reception with the president.

“If those bans are enforced, many of the people vying for a seat at the president’s table don’t live in the United States,” said Public Citizen research director Zach Everson.

Trump’s memecoin events have drawn scrutiny over whether foreign buyers can essentially buy access to the president. Democratic lawmakers called on the White House to release the guest list for the first dinner in May 2025, while some joined a protest outside the golf club. They renewed the request again in October.

FastX, a Singapore-linked crypto trading platform, was the top-ranked wallet, holding $1.65 million in TRUMP at the time of the snapshot on Nov. 16.

The third highest ranked wallet has been linked to Unitas, a stablecoin issuer run by a British Virgin Islands company, according to Public Citizen.

Morten Christensen, a crypto entrepreneur from the Netherlands and founder and CEO of AirdropAlert, shared a picture from the Trump gala dinner on X. He came 26th with $45,351 in time-weighted TRUMP holdings.

Public Citizen also identified 14 wallets it suspects were controlled by the same person or group. Each received approximately 3,700 TRUMP tokens from Binance in October before being emptied weeks ahead of the cutoff.

The gala dinner comes even as the TRUMP token trades 98.8% below its all-time high of $75.35.

Trump held the first dinner for TRUMP holders in May 2025 at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, when the token was trading at $14.43. By the time he held his second memecoin event, a conference and luncheon at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, the token had already dropped to $2.88.

As of the time of writing, the TRUMP token is trading at $0.89.

"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in the statement. "I can't wait to get back to work."

Hours earlier, Huang had offered to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company "and America." His comeback had drawn support from President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, even as CNBC reported that directors were not considering it.

The independent directors' committee investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort "will proceed to conclusion," Nvidia said, and Huang has said he will cooperate with it.

The company also pointed to its new National Security and Export Control Committee, made up of independent directors, and said it is searching for a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company. Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. House committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview on December 1, and Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-SC) has asked him to testify at a public hearing on December 3.

Nvidia shares rose to over $160 in premarket trading on Monday, up about 28% from Friday's close of $125.53, according to Yahoo! Finance. That would add roughly $780 billion to the company's market value, but still leave the stock below its $166.19 close on the day Huang resigned.

#4932. Billionaire Bill Ackman warns Fed will make a rate ‘mistake’ in December

Markets and economists widely expect the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in its December meeting.

Billionaire investor Bill Ackman warned Sunday that the Federal Reserve risks pushing the US and the world into recession if it keeps raising interest rates to try to bring inflation back to 2%, arguing that financial conditions have already tightened “massively.”

In an X post, the hedge fund manager argued that the required investment in global military spending, tariffs, and massive investment in AI infrastructure and energy means that 3% inflation should be a more realistic target for the Fed.

“The Fed will put the US and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” he said.

Ackman’s comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cited hawkish remarks from Fed officials as one factor behind last week’s stock market sell-off.

“Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they overtighten,” Bessent told CBS on Sunday.

The warning comes as Federal Reserve officials remain divided on rate hikes.

In October, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in a 10–2 vote in October, with both dissenters favoring a quarter-point hike.

One of the dissenters was Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, who on Friday argued that financial conditions were still too accommodative to bring inflation back to 2%.

She said it was estimated that inflation reached 3.8% in October and warned that delaying rate increases could force the central bank to raise rates more sharply later.

“In a different environment, the Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury,” she said.

The next decision is due Dec. 9, with CME FedWatch putting the odds of a December quarter-point hike at about 91.2% at the time of writing.

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès questioned Pump.fun’s description of the process as end-to-end encrypted.

Solana-based trading platform Pump.fun’s plan to end external wallet sign-in on the web has drawn criticism over its request that users import private keys to keep their existing wallet-linked accounts.

Users can sign in with an email address or opt for social logins through Google, Apple, or GitHub instead of connecting an external wallet such as Phantom, Solflare, or Ledger, according to a statement.

After Nov. 30, users who access Pump.fun through an existing wallet session will be prompted to add an email or social login, the platform said, adding that their accounts and funds will remain intact.

Pump.fun said private keys imported during the migration process are encrypted in the browser and held by its login provider, Privy.

Meanwhile, Google sign-in will not work inside wallet browsers, including Phantom's in-app browser, and users might need to sign in with email or switch to Safari or Chrome, Pump.fun said.

Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès objected to the migration in posts on Sunday and Monday. According to his analysis, Privy’s infrastructure decrypts and holds imported keys, which he argued makes Pump.fun’s description of the process misleading.

"Calling this 'end-to-end encryption' is misleading at best," Karpelès wrote in a post. "End-to-end encryption means only you can decrypt. Here the encryption does happen in your browser, but the decryption key belongs to Privy: their infrastructure (a TEE) decrypts your private key, keeps it, and signs with it for whoever passes their login check "

Karpelès argued that requiring users to copy and paste their private keys was illogical because the platform already uses standard "Sign in with Solana" cryptographic messages to verify users.

The migration affects only web sign-in. It does not alter users’ wallet addresses, positions, callouts, followers, or usernames, according to Pump.fun. The mobile app, API sessions, and trading are unaffected.

The catalyst was Nvidia’s announcement that its founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. The board voted unanimously just six days after publicly ruling out his return—and even doubling down on their decision several times.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in the statement. Kress will remain chief financial officer, and Jones will stay on as board chair.

“It tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too big to be fired,” Interactive Brokers strategist Steve Sosnick told Reuters.

Prediction markets were caught off guard, too. A Polymarket contract on Huang rejoining Nvidia by November 30 traded near 99% after the announcement, compared with roughly 3% shortly beforehand.

His return also tanked the probabilities of the AI bubble bursting. After his outsting, Polymarket odds skyrocketed to more than 70%, minutes after his reinstatement, the odds dropped to 14%.

The rally followed an ugly stretch for AI stocks. Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, about 47.5% below its October high, while the Nasdaq lost roughly 10% over the previous week. Bitcoin fell toward $55,100 Friday night before staging a weekend recovery.

Monday’s bounce pushed Nvidia above the $166.19 closing price recorded on the day Huang resigned. Bitcoin, meanwhile, recovered the $63,000 area, but its daily chart still shows a bearish moving-average configuration and a relative strength index near 34, indicating that the recent relief rally has not erased the broader downtrend.

Overall, crypto traders are still timid but evidently don’t think this is the end of the world.

On the chart, Bitcoin faces initial resistance around $65,030, followed by $68,090. On the downside, $61,240 and the psychological $60,000 mark are immediate levels to watch; another break lower would put the recent $55,100 area back in focus.

One of the few notable losers was Anthropic, whose stock slipped 3.16% to $85.81. That left the Claude developer about 25% below its post-IPO peak near $115, although still slightly above the $83 offering price set for its $81.34 billion public offering last Thursday. Nvidia itself committed about $10 billion to a separate, conditional private investment in Anthropic alongside the IPO.

The decline looks more like investors continuing to digest a pricey, volatile listing than a reaction to Huang’s reinstatement. #4924. Bitdeer Sells All 281 Bitcoin It Mined Last Week, Holds None

Bitdeer sold every bitcoin it mined last week and still holds none of its own, the company said in its latest weekly update, continuing a nearly year-long strategy of turning production into cash after a weekend plunge in the bitcoin price.

The Singapore-based miner reported output of 281.1 BTC and sales of 281.1 BTC for the week, for a net addition of zero. Its pure holdings, which exclude customer deposits, were zero as of Nov. 20.

The sales came as bitcoin fell to a weekend low of $55,106 early Saturday at 1:17 AM ET, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows. The price has since bounced to near $62,700 as of 11:23 AM ET Monday.

Bitdeer’s treasury shrank from roughly 2,000 BTC at the end of 2025 to zero by Feb. 20, when Bitcoin Magazine reported the miner had liquidated its reserve over eight weeks. At the time, the company said the move should not be a concern for the broader market.

Bitdeer’s filings show how little it has kept since. In its third-quarter results, filed with the SEC on a Form 6-K on Nov. 10, the company listed 47 BTC held at Sept. 30, down from 2,029 a year earlier.

Its September production update showed 61 BTC held at the end of August. The company mined 1,355 BTC in September and 3,855 BTC in the third quarter, compared with 1,109 BTC in the same quarter of 2025.

Bitdeer has grown its fleet quickly. Self-mining hashrate reached 82.3 exahashes per second in the third quarter, up from 35.0 a year earlier, with another 28.7 exahashes per second of co-mining at third-party sites, the quarterly report shows.

The economics are tight. Self-mining generated $217.5 million in revenue in the quarter but only $6.2 million in gross profit. Electricity averaged $47 per megawatt-hour, and the fleet ran at 15.4 joules per terahash.

Bitdeer posted record revenue of $320.7 million and adjusted EBITDA of $69.6 million, but a net loss of $125.5 million. That included a $54.6 million non-cash loss tied to a bitcoin-collateralized loan from a related party.

Bitdeer also reported $213.7 million in cash and restricted cash, and its board authorized a new $100 million share repurchase program on Oct. 8.

Not every miner is selling. American Bitcoin secured a $150 million revolving credit line from FalconX on Monday that is backed by its bitcoin. The company said the facility lets it raise cash without drawing down its reserve.

The loan carries a 5.95% fee and an initial collateral ratio of 143%. Fully drawing it would require about $214.5 million in pledged bitcoin. American Bitcoin has not said whether it has drawn on the line, and its release lists the risk that pledged coins could be liquidated if prices fall.

American Bitcoin, which is majority-owned by Hut 8, said on its Nov. 4 earnings call that it held 8,427 BTC at the end of September. The company has also sold part of its production to cover operating costs.

Other miners have gone the other way. MARA sold 13,597 bitcoin earlier this month, as miners facing thin margins turned to their treasuries for cash.

Shares of Bitdeer (BTDR) were trading near $3.44 at 11:23 AM ET, up about 16% from Friday’s close of $2.96. The stock has ranged from $3.26 to $3.71 on the day as a broad market rally lifted bitcoin-linked stocks after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang.

Bitdeer has not said whether it plans to rebuild a bitcoin position. It said in February that selling was a liquidity measure tied to evaluating powered land acquisitions and scaling its infrastructure.

The company is also shifting toward AI cloud services, and it reported an AI cloud revenue backlog of about $2.9 billion in its third-quarter release.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $62,700.

Just ahead of the announcement, Polymarket put the odds of Huang rejoining Nvidia by the end of the year at just 10.5%, and 2.5% before the end of this month.

Nvidia (NVDA) climbed more than 30% at one point in pre-market trading to around $164, a move that continued into early morning trading on Monday. The move helps alleviate a torrid trading period for the company, which has seen its stock fall around 43% over the past month amid Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, amid reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia had appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while the board considered internal and external candidates, and as recently as Tuesday's quarterly earnings call, said it did not intend to reinstate Huang despite growing calls for him to return as its stock price plunged.

President Donald Trump was one of Huang's strongest supporters during the period, and said Monday that the board had "made the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him as CEO.

"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," President Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

In a statement on Monday, Nvidia said the reinstatement was effective immediately and was the result of a unanimous decision by the board.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," it said.

Chair of the board Harvey C. Jones said Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and his reinstatement is in the best interests of the company's stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.

“I am honored to return to Nvidia," Huang said. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

The board confirmed that, in light of reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the independent investigation it had already launched would continue. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it, the board said.

Jensen Huang’s Wealth Rises $36 Billion as Nvidia Surge Burns Short Sellers for $12 Billion

Jensen Huang’s net worth surged by more than $36 billion on Monday after Nvidia’s board reinstated him as CEO, a dramatic reversal that sent the chipmaker’s stock rocketing and handed its short sellers their worst day in years.

Nvidia shares jumped more than 33% in Monday morning trading, to around $167, recovering the ground lost after Huang resigned 11 days earlier amid a scandal over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials reportedly suspected of spying for China.

The rebound added roughly $36.6 billion to Huang’s fortune, according to Forbes, lifting the co-founder, who owns an estimated 3.5% of Nvidia, to 13th on its global wealth ranking.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

On the other side of the trade, investors betting against Nvidia were nursing about $12.2 billion in paper losses, their biggest single-day hit since at least 2019, according to data firm ORTEX cited by Reuters.

The reversal wiped out more than $10.5 billion in gains those short sellers had booked just last week. Still, ORTEX noted the bears remain up roughly $14 billion since Oct. 29, and with only about 1% of Nvidia’s float sold short, co-founder Peter Hillerberg characterized the move as a reaction to the news rather than a full short squeeze.

The catalyst was Nvidia’s board voting unanimously to bring Huang back, less than two weeks after his abrupt exit. The return followed President Donald Trump publicly pushing for it, with the president saying the board had sought “assurance on the national security threat” tied to the espionage allegations.

The reinstatement rippled well beyond Nvidia. The news lifted the broader market and dragged crypto up with it, with Bitcoin rallying as risk appetite returned, even as Anthropic shares sank.

The S&P 500 climbed about 5% and the Nasdaq rose nearly 7% on Monday morning, clawing back losses from a Friday selloff driven by anxiety over AI spending.

The episode caps one of the strangest corporate sagas in recent memory: a founder toppled by a spy-tinged scandal, replaced, then restored within days as the president intervened and markets whipsawed on every turn.

For Huang, it marks a remarkable personal recovery, his wealth and his role both snapping back almost overnight.

For Nvidia, whose chips underpin both the AI boom and the data centers increasingly entwined with crypto, the saga is a reminder of how much the market’s fortunes hinge on a single company, and a single person.

Sky Protocol cofounder Rune Christensen said on Monday that he could potentially sell a portion of his SKY tokens to institutions to repay roughly 77 million USDS in outstanding loans.

This comes as Christensen tweeted Monday that his borrowing led to a withdrawal crunch in Sky's stUSDS lending pool.

Christensen said he had so far repaid around 3 million USDS. Sky's dashboard currently shows $0 available for withdrawals, with 99.99% of the roughly $159 million pool in use and an annualized depositor rate spiking to over 50% from around 6% earlier in the month.

"This is on me," Christensen wrote, saying he had grown overconfident and borrowed without properly considering "what happens if rates spike."

I've just repaid 3M USDS from my Staked SKY borrow positions. I still owe about 77M. To repay the rest, I'm exploring options to sell part of my SKY directly to institutional investors who share Sky's vision of becoming infrastructure that institutions can rely on. That's the same path that made Sky the only stablecoin protocol rated by both S&P and Moody's. I will aim to post continuous updates as the payback happens. This is on me. I got overconfident in Sky's strength borrowed without properly thinking through what happens if rates spike. it was a big mistake, and it's part of why stUSDS can't withdraw today. I'm sorry. What happens next for stUSDS holders: * I am aware of a proposal being made by the governance participants of Sky that will address the stUSDS situation more broadly. * Until then I will be posting updates at least every 48 hours, even when there's nothing new. USDS is holding its peg. stUSDS holders deserves the best possible outcome this situation, and getting them there is my top priority.

Formerly MakerDAO, Sky lets users deposit its USDS stablecoins into the pool in return for stUSDS. The deposits fund loans to borrowers who put up staked SKY as collateral. But with all the USDS lent out, depositors need to wait for borrowers to either repay loans or make new deposits before they can redeem through the pool.

USDS was still trading near $1 at the time of publication.

An ecosystem proposal posted to Sky's governance forum on Monday called for cutting stUSDS rates to 10%, pausing new borrowing and using the protocol's reserves to buy stUSDS on the open market.

Separately, South Korean exchanges Upbit, Bithumb and Coinone put SKY and USDS on trading warning lists and suspended deposits for both. Coinone cited the risk of losses for stUSDS holders and said withdrawal restrictions were ongoing.

#4906. ‘MoldyRoost’ ads can steal crypto wallet recovery phrases from iPhones

The campaign used at least 480 ad domains to target users in more than 47 countries and could infect a vulnerable iPhone with a single tap.

Hackers are using fake ads to spread malware that can steal crypto wallet recovery phrases from vulnerable iPhones, cybersecurity company Confiant said Friday.

Confiant, which calls the campaign MoldyRoost, linked at least 480 ad domains to it between May 12 and Nov. 17. The ads targeted users in more than 47 countries.

“Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected,” Confiant said in its report.

Google Threat Intelligence reported in March that hackers were using a tool called Coruna to target visitors to fake crypto sites. MoldyRoost bought ads to spread the same tool on sites unrelated to crypto, where tapping an ad could expose a recovery phrase saved on a vulnerable iPhone.

Coruna can search Apple Notes for wallet seed phrases and read QR codes in saved images. A thief who gets a seed phrase can use those words to open the wallet on another device and move the funds.

The campaign also used DarkSword, another tool that can steal wallet data, which Google researchers also warned of in March.

In a Nov. 6 warning about DarkSword, blockchain security firm CertiK urged iPhone users to update their software and keep seed phrases out of Notes, photos and screenshots. It also advised avoiding unfamiliar links and using a hardware wallet for larger holdings.

#4904. CFTC prediction market rules advance to White House review amid state-federal jurisdiction fight

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

In June, the CFTC proposed new rules to delineate its jurisdiction over certain bets made on prediction markets, as those platforms have grown on a massive billion-dollar scale.

A proposed set of rules by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to further assert its oversight of prediction markets is now with the White House for review.

The agency filed "Prediction Markets; Public Interest Determinations" with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), a division within the Office of Management and Budget that reviews federal regulations before publication.

"Staff is considering recommending that the Commission propose rules relating to prediction markets to help clarify the regulatory framework for event contracts and provide greater certainty to market participants," according to the filing on OIRA's website.

In June, the CFTC proposed new rules to delineate its jurisdiction over certain bets made on prediction markets, as those platforms have grown on a massive billion-dollar scale. The agency's proposed rules would restrict event contracts tied to gaming, war, terrorism, and assassination. Over 1,300 comments have been filed on the proposed rule.

When it comes to a controversial spot between states and the federal government — sports contracts — the CFTC says it's their game despite pushback from state regulators.

Under Chair Michael Selig, the CFTC has maintained that it holds "exclusive jurisdiction" over event contracts. Through proposed rulemaking, the agency has argued that prediction market contracts constitute swaps because they are tied to future events, placing them under federal regulation rather than state laws.

States, however, contend that prediction market platforms are effectively operating illegal gambling businesses while avoiding state regulatory requirements and tax obligations. The dispute has escalated into a series of lawsuits involving nearly a dozen states and the CFTC, with courts reaching conflicting conclusions.

Citing those conflicting rulings, former CFTC Commissioner Christy Goldsmith Romero said last Thursday that the case could reach the Supreme Court.

"I think it's likely that the prediction markets may end up losing on the sports contracts," she said at the Capitol Crypto Forum.

On Friday, a coalition of 44 attorneys general said they opposed the CFTC's prediction market rulemaking. New Jersey has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to hear the case and decide whether the federal government or states have jurisdiction.

#4903. Bitcoin Price Fades Near $61,000 as Stocks Soar on Huang’s Return

The bitcoin price slipped back to near $61,100 on Monday afternoon, giving up nearly all of its morning spike even as Wall Street held one of its biggest rallies in years on Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

Bitcoin jumped above $64,000 shortly after the Nvidia news broke before 10 a.m. ET and topped out near $64,500. The move reversed within hours, and the bitcoin price dipped to around $60,800 by 2:45 p.m. ET. It remains up only modestly on the day.

The round trip was costly for leveraged traders. Bitcoin liquidations reached about $321 million, with short bets making up $224 million of that total. Liquidations across the broader crypto market topped $762 million.

Stocks kept climbing while bitcoin slid. The Nasdaq Composite was up about 6.9% near 24,170 at about 3:40 p.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained about 5% and the Dow rose about 3.2%. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days before Monday.

Nvidia (NVDA) led the move, trading near $165.66, up about 32% from Friday’s close of $125.53. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, 12 days after he resigned.

A stronger dollar may be weighing on the bitcoin price. The dollar index rose about 0.65% to 104.40, its strongest level since April 2025, as the stock rebound put more Federal Reserve rate hikes back in play. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point hike remains the base case.

Adam Haeems, head of asset management at Tesseract Group, pointed to steady selling during U.S. market hours since Huang first stepped down. “Bitcoin has fallen in seven of the eight U.S. sessions since Huang went, today’s included, and last week each session’s fall lined up with that day’s ETF outflow,” he said.

Crypto stocks held up far better than the bitcoin price. Strategy (MSTR) was up about 9.3% near $85.03 in afternoon trading, after it disclosed a purchase of 457 bitcoin last week. Coinbase (COIN) gained about 6.7% to near $108.78, Robinhood (HOOD) rose about 8.8% to near $67.64 and Circle (CRCL) added about 8% to near $51.33.

Miners with AI data center businesses posted the biggest moves. IREN (IREN) jumped about 23% to near $14.57, CleanSpark (CLSK) rose about 12.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) gained about 10%. Core Scientific (CORZ) climbed about 9.4% and Riot Platforms (RIOT) added about 7.1%.

Monday’s spot bitcoin ETF flows are the next test. The funds lost about $1.79 billion last week, their fourth straight week of net outflows, as bitcoin slid toward $58,000 on Friday and hit a weekend low near $55,100.

“Tonight’s ETF flow figure is the first real test of this bounce,” Haeems said. Strong inflows would suggest buyers are returning, while another round of outflows would raise doubts about how far the rebound can run.

Traders also face Wednesday’s inflation data and thin trading around Thanksgiving in a holiday-shortened week. Wintermute OTC trader Jasper De Maere said he isn’t ready to call a bottom for the bitcoin price. “A few days of data do not confirm a trend and these series turn slowly,” he said.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,100.

#4901. Perps and Swaps: How to Trade the News on Decrypt

Perps and Swaps: How to Trade the News on Decrypt

Readers have traditionally learned about markets in one place and traded them in another. A story about Bitcoin, a public company or a commodity might shape a view, but acting on it meant opening an exchange or a trading app and starting over.

Decrypt set out to close that gap in September 2026, when it announced The Information Exchange: a network that brings together news, data, market prices, probabilities and the ability to trade, around the subjects readers follow.

The Information Exchange sees Decrypt delivering both the reporting and the market infrastructure that links information to trading, while the Solana blockchain provides the network on which trades settle, including token swaps and perpetual futures.

This guide explains what each one is and how to trade it on Decrypt.

Everything on The Information Exchange runs through a Decrypt Money Account, which launched on Solana in October 2026.

A Money Account holds one balance that funds every product on Decrypt: swaps, perpetual futures and prediction markets.The account is self-custodial, meaning Decrypt does not hold users' private keys and cannot act on their behalf. It is designed to work without seed phrases, and network fees are covered, so users don't need to hold SOL, Solana's native token, to pay for transactions.

A swap exchanges one token for another at the current market price. Instead of placing an order on an exchange and waiting for it to fill, the trader sends one token and receives another in a single transaction.

Swaps on Decrypt are powered by Jupiter, a Solana trading platform that offers swaps, lending, borrowing, perpetual futures and portfolio tools. Jupiter finds prices across Solana's trading venues, so users don't need to choose where a trade is executed.

At time of publication, swaps cover a select group of major cryptocurrencies and Solana tokens, as well as tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets.

As of November 2026, the Assets panel of the Portfolio page groups holdings into crypto, stocks, commodities and collectibles, and lists tokens including SOL, BTC, ETH, XRP and HYPE.

Perpetual futures, or perps, are contracts that let traders bet on whether an asset's price will rise or fall without owning the asset. Unlike traditional futures, they have no expiry date. A trader who expects the price to rise goes "long," and one who expects it to fall goes "short."

Perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets a trader control a larger position than their deposit would otherwise allow. Leverage magnifies gains and losses alike, and if the market moves against a position far enough, it can be liquidated, or closed automatically, wiping out the trader's margin.

Perps on Decrypt are powered by Phoenix, a fully onchain perpetuals exchange on Solana developed by Ellipsis Labs—making Decrypt the first media platform to offer perps trading alongside its journalism.

As of November 2026, Phoenix offers more than 100 perps markets on Decrypt, covering crypto, U.S. stocks, gold and pre-IPO companies. Markets trade around the clock, with leverage of up to 40x, according to Phoenix.

Decrypt plans to keep adding products to The Information Exchange, including Situation Rooms: pages that combine breaking news, live data, prices, probabilities and trading around a single subject.

Decrypt operates The Information Exchange, Decrypt Money Accounts and the swaps, perpetual futures and prediction market products described in this guide.

Perpetual futures are leveraged products and carry a high risk of loss. Availability may vary by region. Nothing in this guide is investment advice.

The U.S. Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture complaint Monday and separately asked a federal judge to keep the assets restrained.

The U.S. Justice Department is seeking to recover about $1.17 billion in USDC tied to the Oct. 29 Binance hack, according to a civil forfeiture complaint seen by The Block. In a separate motion also seen by The Block, prosecutors asked a federal judge to keep the assets restrained.

The amount comes from the balances listed in the complaint, filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. U.S. investigators attributed the theft to North Korean military hackers identified in the complaint as Lazarus Group/Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38).

Prosecutors obtained a temporary restraining order on Nov. 12. In Monday's motion, they said it was unclear when or whether the earlier order would expire and asked for a new order "so that there is no lapse in the restraint of the Defendant Property."

Circle has blocked access to the USDC but told prosecutors it cannot transfer the original tokens from the blocked addresses. The complaint says Circle "has agreed to voluntarily issue new USDC in an amount equivalent to the amount of the Defendant Property" and transfer it to the United States "upon receipt of an Order of Forfeiture from the Court."

In its Nov. 12 announcement, the DOJ said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion tied to the hack. The DOJ said Monday that U.S. authorities have helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto since the theft.

"Following the Binance theft, the FBI and our partners moved quickly to trace and freeze stolen assets and share critical information with virtual asset service providers," said Brett Leatherman, operations director of the FBI's Cyber Branch.

Binance put the losses from the hack at about $6.34 billion and said it fully replenished the affected assets at its own expense. The exchange separately obtained a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing order from an Abu Dhabi court as part of its effort to recover the stolen funds.

#4897. Strive (ASST) Buys No Bitcoin Last Week, Holdings Stay at 43,404 BTC

Strive (Nasdaq: ASST) bought no bitcoin last week and sold no stock to fund new purchases, leaving its holdings unchanged at 43,404 BTC, according to a Monday 8-K filing.

The Dallas-based company reported that its bitcoin count was unchanged between Nov. 13 and Nov. 20. It sold no Class A common shares, no SATA preferred shares and no SATS preferred shares in its at-the-market programs from the Nov. 13 close through the Nov. 20 close.

The pause follows a slowdown from the October sprint that built the stack. Strive bought 251 bitcoin for $17.5 million the prior week at an average of $69,853 per coin, after adding just 29 coins the week before that.

Bitcoin traded near $61,000 on Coinbase on Monday afternoon. That is about 12.6% below the $69,853 average Strive paid for its most recent purchase. At that price, the 43,404-coin stack is worth roughly $2.65 billion.

The filing gives no reason for the pause, and the company has not said whether it plans to resume weekly buying. Strive has typically disclosed its holdings on Mondays, so next week’s update will show whether the stack grows again.

Most of the stack was built quickly. Strive held 28,000 bitcoin on Sept. 30 and acquired 15,124 more between Oct. 1 and Oct. 30, including a single 6,182-coin purchase. The company closed a registered offering of 7 million SATS shares on Oct. 20 for about $609 million in net proceeds, which funded much of that run.

Strive’s cash and cash equivalents slipped to $462.4 million as of Nov. 20 from $465.3 million a week earlier, a decline of $2.9 million. The filing does not break out what drove the change.

The company also still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s variable-rate STRC preferred stock. The fair value of that position fell to $47.3 million from $50.5 million, a drop of about $3.2 million, with the share count unchanged.

Share counts were also flat. Strive reported 118,133,002 Class A shares and 9,198,107 Class B shares, for 127,331,109 effective common shares. Outstanding preferred stood at 14,030,176 shares of SATA and 7,141,037 shares of SATS, the 15% perpetual preferred it has used to fund most of its purchases.

Strive’s holdings rose from 43,153 bitcoin on Nov. 6 to 43,404 on Nov. 13, and the filing shows no change since. With no common or preferred stock sold, the company raised no new capital through its offering programs last week, which left cash as its main resource for dividends and operations.

Strive shares were trading near $15.55 at 3:56 p.m. ET on Monday, up about 7.1% from Friday’s close of $14.51, according to Yahoo Finance. The stock opened near $17.64, a gain of more than 20%, and gave back much of it through the session.

The swing tracked bitcoin-linked stocks broadly after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang and sent equities sharply higher, a move Bitcoin Magazine covered earlier Monday. Bitcoin spiked above $64,000 in the morning before sliding back toward $61,000 during U.S. trading hours.

The stock has lost much of its October run. ASST closed at $30.75 on Oct. 21, so Monday’s price is about 49% lower. It is still roughly 5% above its 2025 year-end close of $14.76.

Strive’s preferred stocks remain a central part of its model. On Nov. 12, the board raised the SATA dividend rate to 13.25% for periods beginning Dec. 1, while SATS continues to pay 15%. Both pay daily cash dividends, so the company’s cash balance funds a steady outflow even in weeks without purchases.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,000.

#4893. Solo Bitcoin Miner Scores Again, Hitting $191,000 Jackpot Against the Odds

Solo Bitcoin Miner Scores Again, Hitting $191,000 Jackpot Against the Odds

A lone Bitcoin miner has once again defied steep odds, single-handedly mining a block and pocketing a reward worth roughly $191,000, a windfall that normally flows to the industrial-scale operations dominating the network.

Blockchain data shows the miner solved block 977057 on Nov. 22, earning 3.12871270 BTC, made up of the 3.125 BTC base subsidy plus about 0.0037 BTC in transaction fees.

The block was found through Solo CKPool, a service that lets independent miners point their machines at the network and keep the entire reward if they get lucky, rather than pooling hash power and sharing payouts.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Solo miners command a tiny sliver of Bitcoin’s total computing power, and finding a block means being the first to guess a winning number against the combined might of massive mining farms running warehouses full of specialized machines.

The odds for a small setup are often likened to winning a lottery, which is why each solo success tends to draw attention.

And yet, it’s far from an isolated event, and solo Bitcoin miners have hit jackpots like this with increasing regularity throughout 2026. Scores worth around $300,000, $225,000, $210,000 and $200,000, as the price of Bitcoin fluctuates, have all landed with individual miners over the past year, some using only modest or rented hardware.

The frequency underscores that while the probability for any single miner is minuscule, the sheer number of people trying means someone occasionally beats the house.

The timing is notable against the backdrop of a strained mining industry. Bitcoin miners have been selling their holdings and pivoting infrastructure toward the AI boom, squeezed by thin margins, a lower post-halving subsidy and a Bitcoin price that has slumped well off its highs.

For large operators, those pressures have made mining a tougher business; for the solo miner who just won, it’s a rare, outsized payday.

What a solo miner does with the reward is up to them, and the win doesn’t change the economics for everyone else still grinding away. But these occasional long-shot victories remain a point of fascination in Bitcoin, a reminder that the network’s lottery, however improbable, still pays out to the little guy now and then.

At current prices, with Bitcoin trading around $62,000, the 3.13 BTC reward works out to roughly $191,000, though the dollar value shifts with the market.

#4888. CFTC staff say bitcoin, ether can count toward derivatives firms’ operating expenses

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Monday, the agency's staff released that advisory and said ether, bitcoin and payment stablecoins could be counted toward that requirement — and would be subject to a haircut.

Staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued an advisory saying certain regulated clearinghouses and exchanges may count cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin and ether toward a requirement to maintain enough assets to cover at least one year of operating expenses.

On Monday, the agency's Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk released that advisory and said ether, bitcoin, and payment stablecoins could be counted toward that requirement — and would be subject to a haircut — a regulatory discount applied to their market value to account for potential losses.

"Pleased to see @CFTC staff continue to provide important clarity around crypto assets in US derivatives markets through today’s staff advisory," said CFTC Chair Michael Selig in a post on X.

The advisory applies to swap execution facilities, clearing organizations and designated contract markets. It also does not create new legal obligations and is not enforceable. The CFTC also noted that crypto do not qualify as cash or very liquid securities under the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — the set of accounting rules used by U.S. companies to report financial statements — so they are not eligible towards a liquidity requirement, which is separate.

Katherine Kirkpatrick Bos, Chainlink Labs' head of legal, called the advisory "significant."

"People don't realize that one of the impediments to these licenses is the cost of holding a lot of $ - this will help," she said in a post on X.

Also on Monday, the CFTC published its final rule creating a reporting framework for certain event contracts. Rulemaking was necessary, the CFTC said, because the agency had previously moved through a no-action letter process and those don't carry the "force of law," and it also wanted to standardize reported data.

The final rule adds a new part regarding clarifying dates for compliance.

“The CFTC will no longer regulate market participants through a patchwork of no-action letters, which serve as band-aids for unworkable regulations," Selig said in a statement. "This final rule is an important step in future-proofing the regulatory framework for event contracts."

#4886. ECB to let banks pledge more tokenized securities as collateral

The ECB aims to start accepting securities issued on platforms licensed under the EU’s distributed ledger pilot program in June 2027.

The European Central Bank (ECB) approved a plan Monday to let banks borrow from euro area central banks against tokenized securities issued on platforms licensed under an EU pilot program.

The ECB plans to put the change into effect in June 2027, according to its announcement. The EU’s DLT Pilot Regime allows licensed platforms to handle trading or settlement of securities using distributed ledger technology.

Since March 30, banks have been able to pledge qualifying tokenized securities issued through central securities depositories that use distributed ledgers. Under Monday’s decision, a bank holding a qualifying bond issued on a licensed pilot platform could also use it to secure a central bank loan.

The securities must still meet the existing collateral rules of the Eurosystem, which comprises the ECB and the national central banks of the euro area. They must also be available to the Eurosystem through an approved link to a central securities depository that offers settlement on TARGET2-Securities, the Eurosystem’s securities settlement platform.

The Eurosystem expects to publish additional legal and operational requirements for the pilot platforms in spring 2027.

“A future-proof collateral framework must embrace new technologies without compromising on safety or the rigour of our risk assessment,” said ECB executive board member Isabel Schnabel.

The ECB said it is also exploring how banks could pledge securities issued and settled entirely on distributed ledgers. Through its Appia project, the Eurosystem plans to publish a blueprint in 2028 for how Europe’s tokenized wholesale financial markets could operate.

#4884. California court terminates lawsuit against Coinbase over TerraUSD purchases

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

A federal judge has granted Coinbase's motion to dismiss a lawsuit brought by Larry Pearl, who purchased TerraUSD on Coinbase in May 2022 shortly before the token collapsed.

A U.S. federal judge has granted Coinbase's Coinbase Global, Inc. (COIN) motion to dismiss a proposed class-action lawsuit brought by Larry Pearl, who purchased the TerraUSD (UST) stablecoin on the trading platform shortly before the token collapsed.

In a Nov. 20 order, U.S. District Judge Maxine M. Chesney granted Coinbase's motion to dismiss. Judgment was entered three days later, terminating the case.

The plaintiff's latest lawsuit, which was the fourth amended complaint, asserted claims under negligent misrepresentation and violations of California's unfair competition, false advertising, and securities regulations.

According to his original complaint in June 2022, Pearl held approximately $13,000 worth of UST on Coinbase at the time of the collapse, which wiped out over 90% of the value of his holdings.

Pearl alleged that Coinbase misrepresented UST by failing to adequately disclose that it was an algorithmic stablecoin linked to sister cryptocurrency LUNA, rather than a reserve-backed asset.

On the consumer-protection claims based on alleged omissions, the court found that Coinbase's website and linked materials had already disclosed that UST was not backed by U.S. dollars held in a bank account and that minting UST required burning LUNA. The court also stated that trading data for UST and LUNA was publicly available.

The court dismissed several claims because they exceeded the scope of the limited leave to amend granted in an earlier order. The remaining claims were dismissed on the merits.

Pearl also alleged that UST was an unregistered security and that Coinbase either sold it directly or materially aided its sale with misleading statements. The court dismissed the securities claims, finding that Pearl failed to show UST was a security under the Howey test. He did not adequately allege a common enterprise or an expectation of profit.

Terra's UST lost its peg amid large withdrawals from the high-yield Anchor Protocol. The failure of the algorithmic mechanism triggered a rapid collapse. UST fell well below its dollar peg while LUNA’s supply hyperinflated, and both tokens lost nearly all of their value within days, wiping out tens of billions of dollars in market value across the Terra ecosystem.

Following the collapse, Terraform Labs co-founder Do Kwon left South Korea. He was arrested in Montenegro in March 2023 while traveling on falsified documents and was extradited to the U.S. in late 2024. In December 2025, a federal judge in New York sentenced him to 15 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to fraud charges.

Kalshi said it 'made the difficult decision' to pause its operations in Utah after a federal judge allowed the state to enforce its gambling laws.

Kalshi has suspended operations in Utah after a federal judge allowed the state to enforce its gambling laws, while avoiding an immediate ban in New York as its court denied the state's request to shut down the prediction market platform.

A Kalshi spokesperson told The Block on Monday that the company "made the difficult decision" to pause its operations in Utah while it awaits a court decision on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's request to block the state from enforcing against Kalshi.

"This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi," said McGavick. "We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated."

The suspension comes amid mounting nationwide legal pressure, as federal regulators and state authorities remained locked in escalating battles over who has the authority to regulate prediction market platforms. The CFTC has maintained that it has exclusive jurisdiction over such platforms under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA), while several states have argued that certain event contracts violate state gambling laws.

Specifically in Utah, U.S. District Judge Robert J. Shelby ruled in August that the CEA does not preempt the state's anti-gambling laws against Kalshi's event contracts, rejecting the company's claim of federal preemption. Kalshi later appealed, but the federal court of appeals denied its request to block Utah's enforcement in September.

Last month, the CFTC filed a lawsuit against Utah and requested the court to temporarily block the state from enforcing its gambling laws against CFTC-regulated prediction markets, including Kalshi. Judge Shelby has not yet ruled.

Meanwhile in New York, a judge has denied Attorney General Letitia James' request to shut down Kalshi, allowing the prediction market platform to continue operating in the state for now.

During a hearing on Monday, New York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane rejected the state's bid for a temporary restraining order (TRO) that seeks to block Kalshi from operating. Kalshi has previously said the potential TRO could shut it down nationwide, though James said that was not her goal.

According to a series of X posts from gaming lawyer Daniel Wallach, the judge said she was uncomfortable granting relief this early in the case, particularly given the scope of the proposed injunction.

"The judge denied the state's request for a TRO, recognizing that there are complex questions about derivatives and preemption," said Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana. "We remain committed to working with the state on a path forward that works for our 1.5 million customers and for the state of New York."

The CFTC and the Department of Justice also sued New York in April, arguing state enforcement actions against prediction market operators are preempted by federal law.

In recent weeks, the CFTC and the DOJ have filed lawsuits against several states, including Utah, Arkansas, and Louisiana, seeking to block state enforcement against prediction market platforms.
