#4879. Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Jensen Huang did not unveil a breakthrough chip on Monday. He simply got his old job back—and Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, while the Nasdaq jumped nearly 7% in midday trading.

The reaction revealed something more consequential than Wall Street’s fondness for a charismatic CEO: investors had spent 11 days confronting how much of the AI boom runs through one person.

Huang, who resigned November 12 amid revelations about extramarital affairs and an unproven Chinese espionage allegation involving a former customer executive, has returned as CEO, president, and director.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Nvidia’s board says his reinstatement poses no national security risk, based partly on input from senior U.S. officials. Its independent investigation, however, is not over.

The company did not stop making chips. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO, Harvey Jones took over as Nvidia’s first board chairman, and executives insisted the technology roadmap and customer commitments remained intact.

Kress presided over earnings that showed roughly $116 billion in quarterly sales and projected about $130 billion for the following quarter—staggering numbers that still failed to calm the market.

Inside Nvidia, the transition looked considerably less routine. During the first companywide meeting without Huang, staff had submitted about 700 questions, many concerning compensation and board transparency.

Kress promised pay increases and extra stock awards in December, months earlier than planned. Executives took turns assuring workers that the company could serve customers without Huang; some employees nevertheless discussed leaving if his absence became permanent.

The pushback extended outside headquarters. An online petition gathered roughly 200,000 names, though signers’ claimed employee or shareholder affiliations were not independently verified. Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, whose firms had disclosed about $2.1 billion in Nvidia shares, urged a deliberate succession process that kept Huang’s return possible. It was an unusual message to directors searching for a replacement: don't rush to replace the founder.

This letter was sent to Nvidia's board today.

Absolutely share @altcap belief that this letter outlines minimum acceptable standards. pic.twitter.com/ST2f5TMAa1

— Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) November 14, 2026

In other words, Nvidia couldn’t survive the scandal—not the one about Huang cheating, but the one about Huang leaving.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and turned graphics processors into the hardware behind modern AI. But his power also lies in the relationships surrounding those chips: cloud giants buying entire data centers of GPUs, developers locked into Nvidia’s CUDA software, suppliers building its next systems and policymakers deciding which markets it can serve.

Reuters reports that he has overseen roughly 60 direct reports and personally shaped major deals and product decisions.

He has also become a financier and ambassador for the AI ecosystem. Nvidia has invested in companies including CoreWeave and Nebius, which buy computing hardware to rent AI capacity to others.

That web of investment, sales, and financing is precisely why his disappearance unnerved markets far beyond Nvidia. After his outsting, Chinese customers delayed or canceled orders while leadership was unsettled; the whole Nasdaq index and the wider S&P500 crashed and odds for a bubble pop spiked to more than 70% on prediction markets.

Then, on Monday, minutes after his return, CoreWeave and Nebius shares each jumped more than 20% alongside Nvidia which had its best day in history—Huang also probably had his best day ever, too.

To have a grasp of Huang’s influence, one just needs to follow the money.

Elon Musk backed the reinstatement campaign; Y Combinator chief Garry Tan and Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney were among other prominent supporters. Bill Ackman celebrated Monday with “sanity prevails.” Trump pressed the case personally, later saying his intervention was “very important” and that the administration assured directors there was no national security obstacle to Huang’s return.

That backing helps explain the whiplash: On November 17, Jones said the board would not reinstate Huang, citing conduct inconsistent with Nvidia’s standards. Six days later, the same directors voted unanimously to bring him back. They say meetings satisfied them about his candor and leadership, but have not explained exactly what changed. Supporters see recognition of an indispensable founder; critics see a board yielding to powerful outsiders.

Bullish analysts argue that restoring Huang reduces execution and talent-retention risk. Dan Ives has framed Nvidia as a $300 stock with Huang versus $225 without him, while Melius Research upgraded the shares to “buy” with a $220 target.

Yet Monday’s roughly 30%-plus rebound followed a Friday close of $125.53; even near $165, Nvidia remains well below its October peak. Buying the comeback means paying much more for the same projected chip sales.

The other side is harder to price. Michael Burry criticized the reversal, and legal scrutiny of Huang, Nvidia’s export controls and its board continues. The company is establishing a board committee for national security and export-control oversight and recruiting a chief compliance officer.

None of that resolves the fundamental AI question: whether customers can earn enough on massive infrastructure spending to sustain Nvidia’s growth.

Huang’s return repairs a missing link between Nvidia, its customers, Wall Street, and Washington. The 11-day crisis showed how much confidence that link carries—and how vulnerable the AI trade becomes when it breaks.

What he has not yet won back is an unquestioned mandate to lead.

#4877. Critics of Netflix’s FTX drama point to Obama’s producer credit

Series creator Graham Moore said he invented a scene in which Changpeng Zhao urges Alameda Research to trade ahead of FTX customers’ orders.

Critics who say Netflix’s new FTX drama favors Sam Bankman-Fried over Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao have pointed to former US President Barack Obama’s role as an executive producer.

DRW founder Don Wilson said Sunday that Netflix’s FTX drama The Altruists portrayed Bankman-Fried too sympathetically at the expense of Zhao.

In the fourth episode, Zhao’s character urges Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison to give Alameda Research advance access to FTX customers’ orders so it can trade ahead of them.

Series creator Graham Moore identified the scene as fiction in a Friday essay for Vulture. Moore wrote that he believed the pressure the pair faced was real, though “there’s no evidence that CZ ever specifically pressured FTX to front-run.”

Zhao called a clip from the series “complete BS” on Friday, a day after the eight-episode drama premiered. Investment research firm Farside Investors also singled out the front-running scene, saying the show cast Zhao as the villain.

Wilson called the clip an “epic fail by Netflix.” In a second post, he cited the former US president’s executive producer credit. Netflix lists both Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers and names Moore and Jacqueline Hoyt as showrunners.

In a Sunday post on X, an account called StarPlatinum pointed to the Obamas’ producer credits and Bankman-Fried’s donations to Democrats. The post did not offer evidence that the donations influenced the show.

Related: Sam Bankman-Fried wrote to actor portraying him in Netflix series

Bankman-Fried made about $40 million in publicly reported political donations during the 2022 election cycle, mostly to Democratic candidates and groups. Federal prosecutors later said he also used FTX customer funds to make political contributions to candidates from both parties.

In November 2022, Zhao announced that Binance would sell its holdings of FTT, FTX’s token.

At Bankman-Fried’s 2023 trial, Ellison, Alameda’s former CEO, said she thought Zhao’s announcement “contributed to the situation.” She said FTX collapsed primarily because Alameda could not repay more than $10 billion in FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2024 for orchestrating a fraud that took more than $8 billion from FTX customers.

FTX’s bankruptcy estate sued Binance and Zhao in November 2024, seeking $1.76 billion paid in a 2021 share repurchase. The estate also sought damages over Zhao’s public statements. Binance called the claims “meritless.”

In July, US Bankruptcy Judge Karen Owens dismissed the claims over Zhao’s statements because FTX’s own misconduct barred them. She allowed the estate to pursue its separate claim over the buyback.

#4874. AI agents are using credit cards. Where does that leave crypto?

AI agents are already using credit cards to transact, raising questions about where crypto fits in the emerging agent economy.

The idea that crypto will become the default payment choice for autonomous AI agents is widespread in the industry. The thesis is that because AI agents can’t open bank accounts and need to make lots of transactions, they will inexorably gravitate to instant, decentralized and low cost crypto payments.But the credit card industry has no intention of letting that happen.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 19 that AI agents are already using credit cards to make purchases on consumers’ behalf, and banks and payment companies are racing to accommodate them. Crypto trader and co-host of the 1000x podcast Jonah Van Bourg posted a screenshot, and commented:

But experts argue the jury is still out. Professor emeritus of finance at Marquette University, David Krause, tells Magazine that credit cards offer some advantages, but high costs could be their downfall in certain scenarios.

Stablecoins, he says, make much more sense for “those situations involving micropayments.”

Credit card payments are the default for most human-initiated transactions on the web. So an agent tasked with booking a flight or a hotel room may also default to this type of payment as well.

Related: DeepSeek developing AI agent requiring less human input: Report

“When an agent books your flight or reorders your groceries, it’s acting for a person, at a merchant that already accepts cards, with consumer protections people expect, like chargebacks,” Lewis Nurcombe, chief revenue officer at WalletConnect, tells Magazine.

Visa’s recent paper on the rise of agentic commerce says tokenization can give agents permission to transact without needing to expose the cardholder’s underlying payment details, and spending controls can restrict the purchases they can make.

So when the merchant already accepts cards and has familiar mechanisms for handling disputed transactions, it’s hard to argue the virtues of introducing an entirely new payment system.

But the economics start to change when agents begin paying other machines.

AI agents may create a new economy of machine-to-machine transactions, where agents buy access to a dataset, request computing power, or pay to access a single piece of information. Many of these transactions may only be worth a fraction of a cent and potentially need to occur thousands of times without a human approving each one.

“If an agent wants to pay a few cents for one API call or one piece of data, card fees don’t make sense,” Aitor Argomaniz, chief executive of AI payments company Nevermined, tells Magazine.

That’s because card networks were designed around transactions big enough to absorb fixed processing fees, rather than micro-payments.

Stablecoins offer a different model. Agents can hold funds in a wallet, make payments programmatically and settle transactions onchain without going through a conventional checkout process.

Nurcombe says that stablecoins are most useful “wherever the transaction is too small, too frequent or too global for cards to make sense.”

x402 is an open, neutral standard for internet-native payments. Source: x402

Nevermined compared 100 API calls priced at 10 cents each. Using a conventional card via Stripe would not be an option as the payments infrastructure network rejects charges under $0.50. But using stablecoins, the company estimates the same 100 payments would cost around 10 cents in total using Coinbase’s x402 facilitator on Base.

That doesn’t mean crypto payments will automatically win however, as a number of microtransactions could be aggregated into a single card payment. Stablecoin transactions also carry costs related to infrastructure, conversion, custody and liquidity.

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) found that stablecoin transfers can still incur trading, conversion and withdrawal fees, while limited liquidity between stablecoins and local currencies can add further friction.

In the transition to agentic finance, there’s a more fundamental question to overcome: who is responsible when an agent gets something wrong?

Related: Banks are banning AI agents over security... and competition concerns

“I tell my students the real question isn’t ‘crypto or cards,’ it’s who solves the agent identity and liability attribution issues,” Krause says.

One partial solution is a separate wallet funded with a limited amount of money that could prevent an agent from accidentally draining a user’s main account.

WalletConnect is developing ways for users to give agents access to dedicated wallets while retaining control over the rest of their funds.

“The most an agent can ever spend is what the person chose to give it,” Nurcombe says.

But spending limits only mitigate the damage. They can’t determine who is liable when an agent makes an unauthorized purchase, buys the wrong service or falls victim to manipulation. Nor do they provide the kind of resolution consumers expect from established payment providers.

Nevermined compared 100 API calls priced at 10 cents each. Source: Nevermined.

That may mean banks and card networks have an advantage beyond just having more merchants on their systems; they already have relationships with customers, businesses and regulators, as well as established processes for handling disputes.

Krause says that stacks the odds in traditional finance’s favor. “My bet is the large TradFi players will ultimately win,” he says. “They’re the ones with funding access and are positioned to straddle the divide and offer a hybrid version.”

Nevermined supports payments using both cards and stablecoins, and Argomaniz expects the two systems to coexist, “at least for the next few years.”

This is where Van Bourg’s argument becomes harder for the crypto industry to dismiss — even if stablecoins are useful for machine-to-machine payments, established payment networks could just incorporate them without handing over control of the customer relationship.

So an agent might interact with Visa or Mastercard while the networks use blockchain infrastructure behind the scenes.

That would effectively turn blockchain into payment plumbing without businesses or consumers needing to hold crypto or interact with a decentralized protocol.

Mastercard completed its acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure provider BVNK in August, in a deal announced at up to $1.8 billion, giving Mastercard the infrastructure to connect fiat and onchain payments.

So, while AI agents could use blockchain-based payments where existing rails struggle, crypto could find itself powering the agent economy without capturing much of its value.

#4873. North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea’s hackers have now funneled at least $247 million from the record $6.4 billion Binance theft through Bitcoin “coinjoins,” a mixing technique designed to sever the trail between stolen funds and their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said.

The figure, roughly a month after the Oct. 29 hack, reflects just the funds pushed into coinjoins, which pool many users’ Bitcoin into a single transaction so the coins can’t be traced.

Notably, almost all of it was coordinated by a single known individual: the operator of Kruw, the most widely used coinjoin coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users. That operator “refuses to block funds such as these,” Elliptic co-founder Tom Robinson told Decrypt in an email, which is why the firm expects the laundering to continue.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The mixing accelerated sharply in mid-November. On Nov. 17, the attacker emptied five of the nine largest Ethereum addresses tied to the theft, shifting about 488,000 ETH ($860 million) into fresh batches.

Those are being steadily swapped into Bitcoin through the Thorchain bridge and then sent into coinjoins, often within hours, the same playbook North Korea used after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in early 2025.

The operation has spanned more than 27,000 wallets across at least 16 blockchains, roughly 55 services and some 90,000 transactions. Elliptic stressed it is clearly automated but found no evidence AI agents are directing it, pointing instead to conventional software, with fixed timing, set amounts and pauses that resemble human working patterns in Pyongyang.

Elliptic earlier found the hackers even minted their own worthless meme coins to shuffle funds through liquidity pools, one of several obfuscation tactics stacked together alongside cross-chain bridges, asset swaps and lending-vault hops.

The FBI has attributed the theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and Binance has said it will cover all customer losses.

Still, little has actually been cashed out. About $2.85 billion has been frozen, and roughly $2.35 billion remains parked in theft-linked addresses, including the 18,270 BTC taken directly from Binance, which hasn’t moved since the night of the hack.

Elliptic expects the funds to be converted to Bitcoin, mixed and eventually cashed out through over-the-counter brokers over a period of months, the point at which they can still be intercepted.

With the Kruw operator declining to block the flows, though, the mixing shows little sign of slowing.

#4869. The Man With No Butt

My flat ass has haunted me since high school. So I did what any man would do and sought out some wisdom from the Internet. This is the story of my midlife butt crisis.

I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. New Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

While other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

The problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

He stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

By high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

“He has no butt!” another voice announced with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:

Sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I said the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”

You have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

The moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

Crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”

I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire company around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”

The search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he said, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”

Ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

As for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he said it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

But the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

Dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

When I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

Derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Big Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he said.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

But then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”

Wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

Dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a big butt and have really weak glutes.”

All these years, I’d associated my small butt with weakness. With inadequacy. With being less than. What if I was wrong? What if, beneath my perpetually drooping pants lurked a superhero-strength posterior more powerful than even Derek’s celebrated Italian ass?

Unlikely. And who am I kidding? It’s not like if I had said to those girls in high school, “Oh no, you don’t understand—it’s really strong!” they would have stopped laughing and made out with me.

But hey, this new knowledge gives me something to cling on to. Wish I could say the same for my pants. Still, I am what I am. I am No-Butt Bender. And if that makes my kids laugh and my wife give me a warm, “It’s okay. I love you anyway” hug, I’ll take it.

Mike Bender is a #1 NY Times Bestselling author of "Awkward Family Photos," screenwriter of "Not Another Teen Movie," and an award-winning children's book author at Random House Children's Books. He recently published a picture book for kids inspired by his health journey called "The End Is Just The Beginning''.

#4868. Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned Sunday that artificial superintelligence is approaching—and that humanity may be unable to control systems far smarter than itself.

In an essay on X titled “Superintelligence is Arriving,” Wang said the next year could determine how people live alongside machines capable of improving themselves. His catalyst was an extraordinary mathematics result involving Anthropic’s Claude.

“Superintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Wang called the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis a greater intellectual achievement than building the atomic bomb, which he described as a “homework problem” by comparison. The breakthrough, he wrote, came with help from an “alien mind that we don’t understand.”

The warning carries extra weight because Wang runs Meta Superintelligence Labs. Mark Zuckerberg brought him aboard in 2025 after Meta invested $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Wang’s startup, Scale AI.

On Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he and Claude had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a conjecture about prime numbers that had resisted mathematicians since 1859. The claim arrived a day after Anthropic’s massive IPO.

Alpöge released roughly 17 million lines of code in Lean, a system that checks mathematical proofs. On Saturday, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified that the code proves the correct statement; researchers are still working to explain its mathematics in conventional form.

For Wang, the result suggests raw reasoning power is no longer AI’s central limitation. He argued that the remaining hurdles involve specialist knowledge, experimentation, and the tools needed to apply intelligence in other fields.

That includes AI research itself. If machines can redesign more capable successors, Wang fears a cycle of recursive self-improvement could move faster than human monitoring or intervention.

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” he wrote. He also questioned human control over hypothetical systems “1000x smarter” than people.

Wang criticized the industry’s “lazy thinking” that superintelligence is inevitable and the only question is making it safe. “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI,” he wrote, advocating technology that strengthens human decision-making.

In a Monday follow-up, he said Meta had delayed its Muse launch for months over safety concerns and backed industry safeguards. Zuckerberg, he added, wants most computing power devoted to serving customers rather than unrestricted self-improvement.

Meta nevertheless has its own ambitions. Its Muse Wonder models, released in October, compete with systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, making Wang both a critic of the race’s direction and a leading participant.

Not everyone accepts his leap from mathematics to superintelligence. NYU professor Andrew Gordon Wilson argued that proving an existing conjecture is different from inventing new mathematical frameworks such as calculus or relativity.

“Nothing compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might”. I disagree. The introduction of calculus, general relativity, and quantum mechanics, are more profound intellectual achievements. Creativity, taste, and intuition is the difference.

— Andrew Gordon Wilson (@andrewgwils) November 23, 2026

The Riemann result demonstrates a remarkable human-AI collaboration, but it does not prove that autonomous superintelligence exists.

Wang has urged the industry to change course while Meta continues developing the systems he fears could eventually exceed human oversight.

#4867. Strategy buys 457 Bitcoin, spends $212M on preferred share buybacks

Strategy raised its preferred stock buyback limit to $4 billion and authorized the transfer of up to $1 billion from its dollar reserve.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy bought 457 Bitcoin for $29.6 million last week and spent $211.8 million buying back its STRC preferred shares, more than seven times what it spent on Bitcoin.

The company paid an average of $64,898 per Bitcoin (BTC) in the week ended Sunday, bringing its holdings to 851,305 BTC, according to Monday’s filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Strategy paid $64.23 billion for those holdings, or an average of $75,446 per Bitcoin.

Strategy raised $176.7 million in net proceeds from sales of its common stock. It used $29.6 million for Bitcoin purchases and $147 million to buy back STRC shares. It funded another $64.8 million in buybacks with cash.

Strategy’s board also raised the limit on preferred stock buybacks from $3 billion to $4 billion, leaving $1.12 billion available for further purchases. The board authorized management to move up to $1 billion out of the reserve it keeps for dividends and interest payments. Strategy can use that cash for other purposes, including buying Bitcoin.

Bitcoin fell to $55,081 on Saturday, its lowest price since September 2024, before rebounding above $61,000 on Monday. Crypto investor Kyle Chassé estimated Saturday that Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings were worth roughly $47 billion, about $17 billion less than the company paid for them.

#4866. The Best Barbour Jacket Alternatives, According to Fashion Editors

You don’t need a designer price tag to pull off one of menswear’s most iconic outerwear styles.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I’M A SUCKER for a good Barbour jacket. I’ve always considered the British heritage brand’s waxed-cotton outerwear the perfect finishing touch to a nicely put-together fall-winter outfit. Founded in 1894, Barbour originally made weather-resistant jackets for sailors, fishermen, and outdoor workers before becoming a staple of British countryside dressing. Over the years, its association with the royal family, including Princess Diana and King Charles III, helped give the rugged outerwear an upper-class appeal. But in the past five years, Barbour has seen a major resurgence, thanks to the barn-jacket boom on runways at Prada, Loewe, and Bottega Veneta, along with a growing appetite for timeless pieces over fast fashion. Buzzy collaborations with designers like Gucci and Paul Smith, plus the popularity of British countryside style in shows like The Crown, have also introduced the look to a whole new generation of guys.

But as much as I love Barbour jackets, dropping several hundred dollars on one isn’t exactly in everyone’s budget. Some of the brand’s most iconic styles, including the Bedale, Beaufort, and Ashby, will set you back anywhere from $415 to $450. And that’s before you dive into the designer collabs. Take the latest J.Crew x Barbour Beaufort jacket. It’s a fresh, reimagined take on the brand’s signature outerwear, dressed in a bold apple-green shade with a weather-resistant finish and tartan lining. Personally, it has me in a chokehold. At nearly $500, it’s a pretty steep investment, especially if you’re just looking to dip your toes into the barn-jacket trend.

Thankfully, you don’t have to spend that kind of money to capture the same British countryside charm. Plenty of menswear brands have put their own spin on the classic barn jacket, offering similar silhouettes, canvas fabrics, and utilitarian details at more digestible prices. I’ve rounded up some stylish Barbour jacket alternatives from brands like Bonobos and Quince that look just as sharp, whether you’re getting dressed up or keeping it casual.

Of all the Barbour jacket alternatives I’ve tested, Quince’s version comes close in comparison to the Barbour x Paul Smith collaboration I already own. That jacket runs north of $800, while Quince’s costs just over a hundred bucks but with nearly all the same bells and whistles: a two-tone brown colorway, contrasting corduroy collar, and snap-button storm throat flap that helps seal out drafts of wind. There’s also a two-way zipper that lets me open the jacket from the bottom when I need a little more breathing room.

It’s made from 100% organic cotton and fully lined with soft cotton flannel, which adds a welcome layer of warmth on chilly days when I can skip wearing a bulky sweater underneath. The cut hits just below the waist, with a roomy fit that leaves plenty of space for layering without feeling overly baggy. I’ve even worn it through a few light rain showers, and the fabric didn’t get soaked. I also appreciate how the classic design makes it easy to dress up with trousers and an Oxford shirt or keep things casual with jeans and boots.

Uniqlo makes one of the best affordable Barbour alternatives I’ve come across, and at just $80, it looks and feels more expensive than it actually is. The lightly padded cotton-nylon fabric provides just enough warmth for temps below 60 degrees. What I especially like is the clean, sleek design that comes with a concealed front closure that hides the buttons and zipper, giving the jacket a sharper, more polished look when fully fastened. There’s also a classic checked lining and two-way flap pockets that can be accessed from the top or sides.

Fit-wise, it has a relaxed, boxy silhouette that hits right at the waist and leaves enough room to comfortably layer a chunky knit over a dress shirt. And unlike some barn jackets that lean heavily into the rugged workwear aesthetic, this one feels a little more understated. It comes in versatile neutrals like olive, khaki, black, and dark brown, so finding one that works with your wardrobe shouldn’t be difficult.

If you’re looking for something that puts a slightly different spin on the traditional barn jacket, Bonobos has you covered. Its Canvas Ranch Jacket trades the usual waxed-cotton construction for a sturdy cotton-elastane blend that has a little stretch, so I’m not feeling boxed in. But what really caught my attention are the angled patch pockets across the front. They’re a subtle departure from the usual straight-cut or flap pockets you see on most field jackets, giving the whole design a more distinctive, modern feel.

The cut extends past the waist and lands around the upper thigh, offering a little more coverage than your typical trucker jacket. I also like that Bonobos keeps the color options simple with midnight navy and forest green, both of which go nicely with denim, chinos, or tailored trousers.

For guys who want the classic Barbour look with a little more protection against the elements, consider this insulated version from L.L.Bean. Unlike some of the lighter options on this list, this one is packed with 60 grams of PrimaLoft Black insulation, a lightweight synthetic fill that helps keep it toasty inside without the bulk of a heavy winter coat. The 100% cotton exterior has a water-resistant waxed finish that will keep you dry in light rain. It also has a quilted exterior that gives the traditional field-jacket silhouette a slightly more outdoorsy vibe.

It’s slightly fitted, so guys who are super jacked might have to size up. But the regular-length cut makes it easy to wear over everyday layers and not feel overly snug. This is a great option for construction laborers, landscapers, and other guys who spend long hours outdoors. It’s more practical than fashion-forward, but you get the timeless look of a heritage field jacket with added insulation and weather protection that make it useful beyond just completing an outfit.

Flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker jacket famously appeared on Pedro Pascal in HBO’s The Last of Us, and we’ve been major fans ever since. This is a burly, no-nonsense trucker jacket made from Martexin waxed sailcloth that’s treated on both sides to help block wind and repel light rain. The antique-finish metal buttons and earthy color options give it that rugged, worn-in look that only gets better with age. On the inside, a full-length blanket-style lining keeps you cozy during 50-degree mornings.

One thing worth mentioning is that the waxed fabric feels pretty stiff at first, so don’t expect it to have that soft, broken-in feel right out of the gate. But that’s also part of the appeal of this type of outerwear. After three wears, the fabric gradually softens and develops more character. Compared to Barbour’s longer field jackets, this one has a more traditional trucker silhouette, so I can pair it with jeans, boots, and other casual staples.

Not every Barbour alternative needs to look like it belongs in the English countryside. Case in point: AYR’s The Club, which takes a more refined approach. It’s made from weatherproofed waxed cotton that offers a water-repellent finish. The fabric is also light enough to wear across three seasons, making it a versatile option for those in-between days when a heavy coat feels like overkill.

I can throw it over a tee with jeans for the weekend or wear it with a collared shirt and trousers to the office. I wore it in light showers, and it didn’t soak through to my clothes. And at a little over $300, it’s certainly not the cheapest alternative on this list. Still, if you’re after something that feels more stylish than rugged, this one makes a strong case for itself.

As the Style and Reviews Editor for Men's Health, Joseph covers all-things fashion and grooming. Previously, Cheatham was a commerce editor for Spy, and he has written for Travel + Leisure.

#4864. OpenAI Will Pay You Up to $8K to Preach the AI Gospel to Small Businesses

OpenAI Will Pay You Up to $8K to Preach the AI Gospel to Small Businesses

OpenAI wants people to spread the gospel of ChatGPT to their local businesses. And it is willing to pay them up to $8,000 a month to do it.

The company launched OpenWorks, a program that recruits AI-savvy individuals and small consulting teams to help neighborhood businesses figure out what to do with the technology. The idea is to move beyond telling a restaurant owner that AI will change everything and actually build something useful for the restaurant.

OpenAI will pay selected partners a monthly stipend of up to $8,000. In exchange, applicants must commit to four full days of free, in-person work with local businesses each month, plus one community workshop. It's not an $8,000 salary just for being good at prompts.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That said, this isn't a full-time job with an automatic $96,000 salary. The company advertises a maximum monthly stipend and asks partners to spend four full days each month providing free, in-person assistance, plus hosting one community workshop.

The application asks candidates to describe a real problem they've solved using AI, what changed afterward, and which businesses they'd help first. Knowing how to give ChatGPT clever instructions apparently isn't enough; experience in coding, automation, marketing or operations helps.

Small businesses pay nothing for the service. They pick a problem, work with a partner on a solution, and get three months of ChatGPT Business at no cost. OpenAI says the pilot covers independently owned U.S. businesses, but leaves out startups backed by venture capital, private-equity-owned companies, and software firms.

The company has some examples to sell the idea. In Fargo, North Dakota, the owners of Tiny Things, a gift shop selling miniatures, used ChatGPT with an OpenWorks partner to build an inventory dashboard. One owner estimated that commissioning a similar tool would have cost about $50,000.

In Charleston, a microgreens grower used the chatbot to find restaurants and write personalized pitches to chefs. He estimates his response rate went from 20% to 75% and says he landed 10 new restaurant customers in four months. Those are the businesses' own accounts, not independently audited results.

OpenWorks is starting in 20 communities, including New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Fargo. OpenAI is inviting applicants elsewhere, too, under the slogan "Help us reach every community in America."

The push comes as the company works to turn consumer enthusiasm into recurring business usage. As Decrypt reported in April, enterprise customers already accounted for more than 40% of OpenAI's revenue, according to the company.

Competition also provides an incentive. Anthropic overtook OpenAI in one measure of business AI adoption earlier this year, even as ChatGPT remained a major consumer destination.

Getting ChatGPT into more neighborhood businesses gives OpenAI another route to paying customers, though the company hasn't said what happens after the free three-month offer. It also follows an October effort with America's Small Business Development Centers to train advisers and reach at least 1,000 businesses through workshops.

OpenAI has not announced a general application deadline or a fixed stipend for everyone accepted. The form is open now, and its most important question is pretty straightforward: Can you actually show up four full days a month and help somebody run a business better?

#4858. Trump-linked American Bitcoin secures $150M credit line from FalconX

The miner can borrow against its Bitcoin to fund operations and expansion after selling about 465 BTC to cover expenses in the third quarter.

American Bitcoin, the miner co-founded by Eric Trump, said in a securities filing Monday that its subsidiary secured a $150 million revolving credit line from FalconX using some of its Bitcoin as collateral.

The subsidiary, American Bitcoin Operating, signed the agreement Wednesday and had yet to borrow against the credit line as of Monday’s filing.

The company said it could use the funds to expand and cover operating costs without selling Bitcoin. In the third quarter, it sold about 465 Bitcoin (BTC) for $36.3 million to cover operating expenses.

The two-year credit line carries a 5.95% annual fee on borrowed amounts and a separate commitment fee on the unused balance. The borrower must initially pledge $1.43 worth of Bitcoin for every dollar borrowed. FalconX can demand more collateral if its value falls below $1.30 per dollar owed.

CEO Mike Ho said the credit line would let the miner “deploy capital and secure the infrastructure that supports our business, while we stay focused on our long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy.” Eric Trump told investors on the company’s Nov. 4 earnings call that its reserve had surpassed 8,500 BTC.

American Bitcoin (ABTC) shares traded at $3.84 in premarket trading at 11:10 am UTC Monday, up 9.7% from Friday’s $3.50 close, according to Yahoo Finance. American Bitcoin shares were down about 94% from a year earlier, adjusted for July’s 1-for-15 reverse stock split. The company said it carried out the split to maintain compliance with Nasdaq’s minimum bid price requirement.

Related: Trumps’ American Bitcoin reports record BTC output, narrower Q2 loss

#4857. China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

Chinese AI developer Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Monday, introducing a new architecture that it claims delivers the reasoning capabilities of models nearly four times its size without requiring nearly as many parameters.

The Beijing-based company says its new 750-billion-parameter model can compete with systems containing two to three trillion parameters. It also supports a one-million-token context window, accepts images and video, and can generate up to 128,000 tokens in a single response, according to its technical documentation. Parameters are the internal values a model learns during training, while tokens are the chunks of text it processes and generates—roughly equivalent to words or parts of words.

The release comes as American companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google dominate the highest positions in AI performance rankings. Chinese developers, meanwhile, have increasingly focused on making powerful models cheaper to run, particularly for coding and autonomous agents.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Z.ai has been among China's strongest competitors. As Decrypt reported in August, its predecessor GLM-5.3 was already competitive with leading American coding models, although it still trailed the best proprietary systems on several software engineering tests.

GLM-5.4 introduces what Z.ai calls a Loop Transformer, which processes information through the same 28 neural network layers twice. Traditional Transformers generally pass information through each layer once, so reusing layers effectively increases computational depth without increasing the number of stored parameters.

The company combines this approach with gated updates, which regulate how much information changes between passes, and a hybrid memory cache that avoids storing an entirely separate copy of previous calculations. Sparse attention also helps the model focus its computing power on relevant information rather than processing everything equally.

In controlled experiments on a smaller 30-billion-parameter model, Z.ai reported that its looping technique increased accuracy on AIME 2025, a mathematics examination benchmark scored by the percentage of correctly solved problems, from 19.17% to 30.42%.

GPQA Diamond, a graduate-level science question-answering test also scored by correct-answer percentage, improved from 47.58% to 56.26%. The experiments required approximately 10% additional training compute, while reducing generated reasoning tokens by 10% to 14% on several tests.

Those results concern the experimental architecture, not independently established performance for GLM-5.4 itself. Z.ai has not published a comprehensive flagship benchmark comparison demonstrating that the new model matches Claude or GPT.

The company is also promoting what it calls Generalized Coding: using programming to accomplish tasks beyond software development. Its demonstrations include building a video game, creating 3D environments, and designing a six-axis robotic arm using engineering software.

The company's previous flagship costs $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output tokens through its API. By comparison, OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol costs $2 and $10, while Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 and $20, respectively.

At those published rates, GLM-5.3 is considerably cheaper than its American counterparts, although GLM-5.4's own API pricing has not been announced. Its actual performance-per-dollar advantage therefore cannot yet be calculated.

China has other serious contenders. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max recently topped Chinese competitors on Arena's agent leaderboard, while Moonshot's Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 have challenged American developers on coding performance and API pricing.

The performance gap remains contested. A U.S. government evaluation placed DeepSeek roughly eight months behind the American frontier, although researchers questioned its methodology.

Z.ai itself remains on the U.S. Commerce Department's Entity List, following its January 2025 designation over concerns that its AI research could support Chinese military modernization. The restrictions limit access to controlled American technology, but have not stopped the company from releasing new models.

How much penetration typically feels good? Those who are unsure should try a smaller G-spot toy rather than a girthier one, says Laino.

Our reviewers only tested vibrators made of body-safe materials, including medical-grade silicone, borosilicate glass, stainless steel, Pyrex, and ABS plastic (for noninsertable parts). “Some materials are much safer for our bodies than others,” says Mintz. “High-quality, medical-grade silicone is not porous, whereas with some toys, you’ve got to be more careful.” Vibrators made from porous materials (like soft rubber) could harbor germs and bacteria, which could lead to painful infections, even if a toy is cleaned regularly.

Many rechargeable vibrators have a battery life of at least one hour, although some toys (like the Womanizer Premium 2) can last up to four hours without a charge. While trying each product, our testers discerned how long the toy could hold a charge, how long it took to charge, and the likelihood of its battery dying mid-masturbation session.

Relatively quiet vibrators are a must for people with roommates, kids, and/or thin walls. While testing, we prioritized discreet vibrators over loud ones; many reviewers compared a vibrator's noise level to others they tested, or have tried in the past. On a related note, many of our testers also preferred vibrators that were easy to stow away or pack for travel, as opposed to bulkier products that took up more space.

Not every product is labeled as a waterproof or splash-proof toy, but many are. Our reviewers put these vibrators to the test in the shower and bath, in order to identify which ones actually hold up in water.

Our team tested vibrators with just three or four speeds and settings, as well as vibrators with unlimited settings. Ultimately, our testers found that the quality of the settings mattered more than the quantity of options—but in some cases, reviewers found that even the strongest speeds weren't sufficient.

Some vibrators can be complicated, so our testers answered a multitude of questions about how straightforward each product was. Was the toy easy to hold and intuitive to use? Were the buttons accessible? Was it seamless to incorporate this vibrator into partnered sex? Was anything about it confusing or uncomfortable? Only the toys that received positive responses earned spots on our list.

Finally, our testers answered the most important question: Did this product feel good, and will they use it again? It's safe to say that all of the vibrators on this list passed the Women's Health vibe check (pun intended).

Over several months, the Women’s Health team, led by lifestyle director Lindsay Geller, researched the bestselling, most popular vibrators for women based on thousands of product reviews and sex therapist recommendations. After identifying the best products of every type and for every budget, our team gathered more than 60 product samples from top-quality brands such as Lelo, We-Vibe, Dame, Magic Wand, Womanizer, and more.

We then tapped 14 Women’s Health editors and professional sex toy reviewers to test out toys from their favorite categories and share their thoughts on which products were the best. Our testers tried the products alone, with partners, and in the shower/bath (if the toy was waterproof) in order to identify the best vibrators for different purposes.

After reading through 52 reviews of our testers’ favorite vibrators, we identified the best product in each category, along with seven runners-up for users with specific preferences, needs, and budgets. Our final products were then vetted by sex and relationships therapist Rachel Wright, LMFT.

If you don’t have a sex toy-specific cleanser on hand, you can always use mild soap and warm water to clean your products, says Mintz. Some toys are even dishwasher-safe. But she recommends investing in an ultra-gentle cleanser that’s designed for sex toys. Plus, she notes, they’re easy to use: “You spray them on, leave them to sit, and then wipe them off.” Just make sure your toy is fully dry before you put it away.

Sex-positive, sex toy-specific online stores such as Lovehoney, Babeland, and Good Vibrations are always great places to start, says Mintz. “I would recommend going to a reputable sex shop that has [customer] reviews,” she says.

High-quality vibrators can be expensive—often, over $100—but there’s a reason you’re shelling out the big bucks. “In general, I would say splurge for a pricier vibrator,” Richmond explains. “Quality control can make a really big difference, and spending a little bit more money is probably going to mean your vibrator will last longer, and have more functional capabilities.”

Generally speaking, expensive products are usually made from better, more body-safe materials. They also have more special features that will seriously enhance your playtime. “With something cheap, the material might be porous, and it might have only one speed or two,” says Richmond. “Something more expensive will be less porous, maybe waterproof, and have more functionality with speeds, Bluetooth connections, things like that.”

Ultimately, “a good-quality vibrator from a good-quality company is a good investment,” says Mintz. That said, it’s okay to try a few mid-priced toys of different categories before splurging on your new go-to luxury product, she adds.

To be clear, there’s no one way to use a vibrator. You don’t even have to use it on your genitals, says Laino. But here are a few ways you can make the most of your playtime, according to experts.

Ahead of partnered sex, you might establish the mood: Light some candles, dim the lights, turn on a sultry playlist. Why not do this before solo play too? “First, find a place and time to relax,” says Laino. “And think about things that are sexy to you.” Your brain is your biggest sex organ, so feeling at ease and worry-free will help you have the best possible time with your new toy, she says.

“Sometimes, just putting a vibrator on your clitoris can be uncomfortable,” Laino says. Using a bit of lubricant can help make the experience more, well, smooth. Just be sure to use a water-based product, as silicone lube can cause microtears in silicone-based toys. You'll also want to avoid any lube that contains irritants like glycerin, petrochemicals, nonoxynol-9, and preservatives.

When using a vibrator, many people head straight to their genitals, says Laino. And while there’s nothing wrong with that, she recommends exploring your body (or your partner’s!) with the toy. “Remember that sexual pleasure can be [felt] all over the body,” says Laino. A few places to try: your nipples, belly, even the backs of your knees.

Some people might want to hold their toy directly against their clit, but for others, that sensation could be too intense. If you’re sensitive, you can use your vibrator over your underwear, or even place a washcloth or bedsheet between your body and the toy to dull the feeling, says Laino.

Want more intensity? Try pressing your vibrator to the upper-left quadrant of your clitoris. It’s “a tiny little millimeter of an area,” but it’s the most sensitive part of the clit, says Richmond. (The more you know!)

Once you’ve found just the right spot, start off with one of the toy’s lower speeds, then go higher, suggests Laino. “A lot of times, people will say, ‘[Masturbating] feels really good, but then I don’t know what to do,’” she says. “At that point, if it feels really good, turn the speed up. And rock your pelvis area—move your pelvic region so you’re in rhythm [with the toy], which can help you have an orgasm.”

Not every toy is waterproof, but if yours is, bring it into the bath or shower. Some people find the sensation of water on their skin erotic, says Laino, which can heighten your masturbation session.

On the flip side, water can also dull the intensity of a toy’s vibrations. “One of the reasons many people don’t like to have sex or use a vibrator in water is because it’s harder to feel things—but for somebody who is very sensitive, it could actually work to their benefit,” Laino adds. It’s all about your personal preferences.

6. Incorporate your toy into partnered sex.

While some toys are specifically designed to be used during partnered sex (hello, hands-free vibrators!), it’s important to remember that any vibrator can be a couples’ vibrator, says Mintz. And no partner should feel threatened by your desire to use a vibrator during sex.

If you’re initiating a conversation about bringing a toy into partnered sex, Laino recommends broaching the topic with a curious—or even flirtatious—tone. You might say: “Hey, I think using a vibrator during sex would be really fun for us. What do you think?”

You can use your toy on your partner, too—even if they have a penis. Try gently teasing their shaft or nipples with your vibe, Laino suggests.

#4851. A Better Airport Outfit Starts With the Basics

We're making a case for putting a little more thought into your travel outfit.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Airports can be a bit intimidating. You’ve got the TSA line to worry about, but more importantly, you have your outfit to figure out. Unfortunately, some people judge what you’re wearing while traveling (it’s me, I’m people). But I also don’t think looking presentable has to be that hard. Some guys show up in full sweats, looking like they're about to spend the next six hours in bed. Others dress like they're heading straight from baggage claim to a dinner reservation. Personally, I think there's a happy medium somewhere in there. You should be comfortable enough to sleep through your flight, but you also shouldn't have to change your entire outfit the second you land. From comfortable pants and breathable T-shirts to stylish sneakers, these are the essentials worth packing for your next flight.

And while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport. We’ve got stretchy trousers that look pretty darn good, a solid pair of sneakers, and layers that work alone or together. It's about finding clothes that do a little bit of everything, especially if you like to travel light.

If you’re looking to spruce up your fit for your next flight (and to become someone’s airport crush), here’s what to know.

I'm not saying you can't wear jeans on a plane, but why would you when you have so many more comfortable alternatives? You'll be sitting for hours, probably in a seat that doesn't give you much room to move, so the last thing you want is a waistband digging into your stomach. Look for pants with a little stretch, breathable fabrics, and a relaxed fit that won't feel restrictive when you're sitting down. Brands like Vuori and DUER have gotten particularly good at making pants that feel like loungewear without necessarily looking like it. And if you're committed to sweatpants, that's perfectly fine, too. Just go for a pair with a cleaner, more structured fit.

Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Relaxed Sweatpant

You really don't need to overthink your airport T-shirt. A good cotton tee will do just fine, especially if it's something you already wear regularly. Personally, I'd avoid anything too tight or made from a heavy fabric, since airports and airplanes can get surprisingly stuffy. A slightly relaxed fit gives you more room to move and makes layering easier, too. I tend to gravitate toward simple, solid-colored tees because they go with practically anything. Uniqlo's AIRism Cotton Oversized T-Shirt is a good example of something that's affordable, comfortable, and easy to dress up or down depending on what else you're wearing.

I don't care if you're flying to Miami in the middle of July; bring a sweatshirt. Airplane cabins have a habit of feeling like refrigerators, and I'd much rather have an extra layer than spend an entire flight shivering. A good crewneck or hoodie is probably all you need, preferably something soft that isn't too bulky to stuff into your bag when you're not wearing it. I'm partial to oversized sweatshirts for traveling, though you don't need to go so big that you're drowning in fabric. Something like Alo's Accolade Crewneck works well because you can wear it with sweatpants or a nicer pair of trousers. And honestly, if you're desperate, a sweatshirt can always double as a makeshift pillow.

Abercrombie SwEssential Popover 2.0 Hoodie

Todd Snyder Champion Relaxed French Terry Crewneck

Eddie Bauer Micro Polar Fleece Lined Pullover Hoodie

Depending on where you're headed, a lightweight jacket might be one of the more useful things you bring. I'm not talking about a huge puffer or anything that'll take up half your carry-on. Think windbreakers, chore jackets, and lightweight layers that you can easily throw over a T-shirt or sweatshirt. If you're traveling somewhere with unpredictable weather, a technical jacket from Patagonia or Arc'teryx makes sense. Otherwise, a simple chore jacket from somewhere like Quince or Gap can make an otherwise basic airport outfit look a little more put-together. Plus, you'll probably wear it during the trip anyway, so it's one less thing to pack.

Quince 100% Organic Herringbone Twill Shirt Jacket

Between getting to the airport, navigating security, and walking what feels like three miles to your gate, you'll probably spend more time on your feet than you realize. That's why I'd prioritize comfortable sneakers over anything else when putting together an airport outfit. You want a pair with good cushioning, enough support, and ideally something easy to slip on and off. New Balance, Hoka, and On all make sneakers that fit the bill, though I'd stick with a pair you've already broken in rather than trying something new on travel day. And since you're probably only bringing one or two pairs of shoes on your trip, bonus points if they match the rest of your wardrobe.

You really don't need much here. In fact, I'd argue the best airport outfits are pretty simple. But a few accessories can make even a basic T-shirt-and-sweatpants combination feel more intentional. A classic Yankees cap from '47 is great for early flights when you don't feel like doing your hair, and a good pair of sunglasses is always useful when you're heading somewhere sunny. I also like wearing a watch when I travel, mostly because I don't want to keep pulling out my phone to check the time. None of these things are essential, obviously, but they're easy ways to make the outfit feel a little more like your own.

Seiko Analog Green Dial Automatic Silver Stainless Steel Watch

#4850. OKX, ICE launch 113 tokenized assets despite issuer objections

The venture named Coinbase and Fidelity among the issuers and asset managers in the rollout after 67 companies objected to having their shares traded on the venue.

OKXICE, a joint venture between cryptocurrency exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), launched a venue Monday for round-the-clock trading of tokenized US securities, with 113 assets set to roll out in stages.

The lineup includes stocks, exchange-traded funds and other exchange-traded products, according to an announcement shared with Cointelegraph. OKXICE named Coinbase, Circle, Fidelity Investments and Robinhood among the issuers and asset managers taking part.

Before the launch, 67 companies, including Meta, Tesla and Netflix, sought to keep tokenized versions of their shares off the venue.

Each token represents a security entitlement backed one-to-one by an underlying share, OKXICE said. Holders are entitled to dividends and voting rights where applicable.

OKXICE said the venue operates under the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s Innovation Exemption. Access is limited to eligible US customers of OKX Inc., who must verify their identity, activate a self-custodial wallet and complete onboarding before trading through the OKX app.

#4848. TikTok’s Viral Winter Arc Challenge Is the Best Way to Get a Jump-Start on Your New Year’s Goals

Here's how to make the most of these last few months of the year.

Between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year. While, yes, you should cut yourself some slack here and there during the busy holiday season, it’s also more important now than ever to finish the year strong.

That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play. This annual challenge, which originally went viral on TikTok back in 2024, starts October 1 and ends January 1 (but if you missed the start, it’s not too late!). The only premise: Stay locked in on your goals for the rest of the calendar year, whether that’s training for a half-marathon, hitting your Goodreads book quota, or mastering a new hobby.

This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, says Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in New York City. Now’s the time for you to “be intentional about your energy and what serves you.”

If you haven’t started the challenge yet, it’s not too late. Whether you try it for 83 or 30 days, the Winter Arc Challenge will set you up for greater success with your New Year’s goals because it’ll strengthen your self-efficacy, or “your sense of belief in your own ability to do what you say that you are going to do,” says Carmichael. Self-efficacy is strengthened through your own behavioral track record, so if you start meeting goals now, you’ll already have momentum heading into January, she explains.

Ready to tackle your own Winter Arc Challenge? Here are some helpful tips to help you make the most of the next few months:

Maybe as part of your Winter Arc Challenge, you aim to cut your monthly spending in half. But a few weeks after setting this goal, you really go overboard at brunches and parties. Don't sweat it. This is “a completely normal part of the change process,” Carmichael says. Instead of giving up when you encounter a relapse here or there, plan for bumps to happen, then get back on track.

So, if you spend too much money one week, instead of falling into a pattern of negative self-talk, replace your thoughts. Carmichael says to plan a script of what you can say to yourself when you relapse, like: “I can still get back on track and feel good about my goals. This is my moment to restart.”

Say you’re planning to work out four times a week until the end of the year. If you know the cold morning weather is going to persuade you to stay under the covers and sleep in, be proactive: Book workout classes online every week so you know they’re in your calendar, and you’re more likely to show up. Also, write down your challenges—like the dropping temps preventing you from leaving your house—to keep yourself accountable, Carmichael adds.

Picture yourself on January 1 having been successful with your Winter Arc Challenge, then move backward and think about everything that led up to it. If your big goal was to do a yoga class every week, visualize yourself walking through the snow to get to your Monday night class, or doing a virtual class at home when there was a bad blizzard. Also think about when you almost skipped classes and fell off the wagon, but you used thought replacements to continue reinforcing your goals. Using imagery will help you mentally prepare for the journey ahead, Carmichael says.

Ask around to see if any of your friends are also doing the Winter Arc Challenge—or if they’re willing to hold you accountable. Then, plan regular meetups or calls to check in. “Talk about how things went with a promise to be honest and supportive if one or both of you is falling off,” Carmichael says. “It will help you to stay consistent when you can leverage your social support network.”

No matter when you started the Winter Arc Challenge, you’ll see and feel the benefits of bettering yourself in no time. Good luck—you got this!

#4847. Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO amid ongoing intelligence probe

Nvidia shares surged nearly 29% after the company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO following consultations with the US government.

Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO after consultations with senior US government officials, concluding that his return posed no national security risk despite an ongoing investigation into an alleged foreign intelligence operation targeting him.

In a Monday announcement, Nvidia said its directors were satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead following a series of discussions. The independent investigation will continue despite his reinstatement.

Nvidia shares surged 28.91% to $161.82 shortly after US markets opened on Monday, according to Yahoo Finance data.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will return to her previous role, while Harvey Jones will remain chair of the board.

The chipmaker also said it had recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprising independent directors to oversee compliance and security risks. Nvidia plans to appoint a chief compliance officer and said it would continue cooperating with government investigations.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a former executive whom US intelligence agencies reportedly believed was passing information to Beijing. Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14% intraday following his departure before recovering some losses.

Days later, Silicon Valley executives reportedly organized a campaign to bring Huang back, including efforts to secure White House support. A public petition calling for his reinstatement had gathered more than 187,000 signatures by Nov. 16.

Despite the campaign, Nvidia’s board was reportedly not considering reinstating Huang, instead focusing on its investigation into his conduct. President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang return, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged the company to appoint an outside leader.

The uncertainty surrounding Nvidia came amid a broader market selloff on Friday, when the Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.28% and the S&P 500 fell 3.69%. Bitcoin (BTC) also dropped below $60,000 for the first time since July, with CoinShares head of research James Butterfill attributing the cryptocurrency’s weakness partly to deteriorating sentiment toward AI stocks.

Related: GTA VI publisher racks up nearly 3x Nvidia’s tokenized stock volume

Huang’s reinstatement comes as he faces ongoing congressional scrutiny over Nvidia’s dealings with China. He has agreed to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1 and separately agreed to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee, although a date for that hearing has not been announced.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren called Huang’s reinstatement “reckless” on Monday, saying Nvidia still owes Congress answers about its compliance with US export controls. She also called on the Trump administration disclose which senior officials provided input in support of his return.
